scoring.rule: Short essay scored against a rubric of five items, 1 point each.

chapters.2: Chapter 2: Game art and sound assets
chapters.3: Chapter 3: 3D assets and the Blender pipeline
chapters.5: Chapter 5: Game design documents and virtual worlds

questions.source: Say it to the agent: frame-rate independence and global state
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction for a game: "Add a global thing so the enemies chase the player every frame at speed 4." Identify at least three words or phrases in it that are too vague for an agent to implement reliably, explain what the agent could build wrong for each, and rewrite the instruction using precise engine terms. Your rewrite must settle how fast the enemies move on screens that run at different frame rates.

rubric.text: Identifies "every frame" and "speed 4" as ambiguous and shows the consequence: 4 units per frame is 240 units per second at 60 frames per second but 576 at 144, so the speed depends on the machine, and the unit is not stated.
Rewrites the speed as a rate per second in stated units, so the same distance is covered per real second at 60 and at 144 frames per second.

Identifies "global thing" as unclear about what it is and where it lives (a script on a node in the level, a manager node, an autoload or singleton that survives scene changes) and names a wrong result, such as state that vanishes when the scene changes.
Names the callback that runs the movement and how it keeps the speed frame-rate independent: a per-frame callback with the step scaled by delta time, or a fixed-step callback.
Gives a final instruction that combines these terms, with a target, a rate in units per second, a named callback and a named location for any shared state.

questions.source: Instance, prefab, blueprint class and overrides
questions.prompt: A level contains 30 copies of a crate. The designer wants the crates in one corner to be heavier, and later wants every crate to play a new sound when hit. Explain the difference between a template asset (a Unity prefab, an Unreal Blueprint class or a Godot scene file) and an instance of it, and use the crate case to say what the designer does for each wish, what an override is, and what happens to the heavier crates if the template's default weight is changed afterwards.

rubric.text: Defines the template asset as the single definition and an instance as a placed or spawned copy, as opposed to 30 unrelated hand-made copies.
Says an instance stays linked to its template, so an edit made to the template reaches the instances instead of being repeated on each copy.
For the sound: edits the template once (adds a component, node or sound setting to it), and all 30 instances receive it without being edited one by one.
For the heavy crates: changes the weight on those instances only, and calls this an override, a value stored on the instance rather than in the template.
Explains that when the template's default weight later changes, instances without an override follow it, while the overridden crates keep their own value until the override is reverted.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a health bar to float 40 units above each enemy's head and to follow the enemy as it walks, turns around, and is scaled up to become a boss. A coding agent proposes to compute the enemy's world position every frame and write it into the health bar's position. Explain local versus world (global) space, propose a better setup using parent and child objects, and say what the child's position values then mean. Explain what happens to the bar if the enemy is rotated or scaled, and how the developer should phrase the instruction so that the agent does not mix up the two spaces.

rubric.text: Defines local space as positions measured relative to the parent and world (global) space as positions measured from the world origin, with the world position derived from the chain of parent transforms.
Proposes making the bar a child of the enemy with a fixed local offset, so the engine carries it along and no per-frame copying is needed.

Explains that the parent's rotation and scale also apply to the child's offset: a rotated enemy swings the bar around it, and a boss at scale 2 puts the bar 80 units up unless the scale is compensated or the bar is kept out of the scale.
Says what the child's position values then mean: they are local, measured from the parent, so the 40-unit offset stays the same while the bar's world position changes as the enemy walks.
Gives a precise instruction naming the parent and child, stating that the 40 units are a local offset along the enemy's up direction, and saying whether scale should be inherited.

questions.prompt: Two players run the same game, one at a steady 60 frames per second and one at a frame rate that varies between 30 and 144. Explain the difference between the per-frame update loop and the fixed-step physics loop, what delta time is, and why a jump can reach a different height on the two machines if jump physics is driven by the per-frame delta. Explain what the engine does when one frame takes longer than the fixed step, and say which loop gravity belongs in and which loop camera smoothing or a UI animation belongs in.

rubric.text: Defines a frame as one pass of the main loop that ends in a rendered image, whose duration varies, and the fixed step as a physics update of constant length run a set number of times per second, with delta time as the time since the previous call.
Explains frame-rate independence: per-frame motion is scaled by delta (speed expressed per second), and in the fixed-step callback the delta is constant.
Explains that integrating motion with a variable delta gives different arcs, collisions or tunnelling on different machines, so physics-driven motion belongs in the fixed-step callback.

States that after a long frame the engine runs more than one fixed step to catch up (for example about three 20 ms steps after a 60 ms frame) and that on short frames some frames run no fixed step, so the two loops do not alternate one to one.
Places gravity, forces and body movement in the fixed-step loop and camera smoothing, visual effects and UI animation in the per-frame loop.

questions.source: Signal, event and delegate versus direct call
questions.prompt: A game has a player, a HUD, an audio manager and an achievement system, and all four must react when the player picks up a coin. A junior developer makes the coin script call each of the four systems directly. Critique this design, then redesign it with the engine's event mechanism (a Godot signal, a Unity C# event or an Unreal delegate). Explain who emits, who listens and what the connection step does, name one thing that can go wrong with events, and say when a direct call is still the better choice.

rubric.text: Explains that direct calls couple the coin to four systems: it needs a reference to each, must change when a system is added or removed, and cannot be reused or tested alone.

Redesigns it so the coin (or player) emits a "coin collected" event, and each system registers its own callback; the emitter does not name its listeners, and data such as the coin value can travel as an argument.
Explains the connect step: a listener registers a function with the signal, event or delegate, and emitting runs the registered functions (immediately by default in Godot and in C# events).
Names a pitfall, such as a listener that was destroyed but never unsubscribed (a stale registration), reliance on the order in which listeners run, or an event that nothing listens to.
Says a direct call is better when a parent commands a child it owns, when there is a single known target, or when a return value is needed, and that events suit announcing what already happened.

questions.prompt: A game must support keyboard and gamepad, let players rebind controls, treat jumping as a single press, and treat running as a held button. Explain what an input action is and how it differs from a raw key or button, describe how polling and event-driven input differ and which fits each of the two controls, and explain what could go wrong if a coding agent is told only "jump when the player presses space". Write the precise version of that instruction.

rubric.text: Defines an input action as a named intent (such as jump) that is mapped to one or more bindings, as opposed to code that checks a particular key or button.
Explains the benefits: players can rebind without code changes, keyboard and gamepad feed the same action, and the game code stays the same across devices.

Distinguishes polling (ask for the current state during an update, which suits a held run button) from event callbacks (called once when the input occurs, which suits one-shot actions), and says which of the two controls each fits: the held run button to polling, the single jump press to an event or one-shot query.
Explains the problem with the vague phrase: it hard-codes one key, ties the game to one device, and does not say whether holding the key should repeat the jump.

Gives a precise instruction: define an action named jump bound to the Space key and a gamepad button, react once per press (a just-pressed query, which is true only on the frame or tick the press began, or an event callback), and define a separate run action read as a held state.

questions.prompt: A game must keep the player's score, the settings and the music player alive as the game moves from one level to the next. Explain what a singleton is for (a Godot autoload, a Unity object kept with DontDestroyOnLoad, or the persistent Game Instance in Unreal), why a developer should not put everything there, and name two alternatives. Say what a developer should ask the agent for instead of "make it global".

rubric.text: Explains the purpose: an object (a Godot autoload, a Unity object kept with DontDestroyOnLoad, or the Unreal Game Instance) that lives for the whole run, outlives scene or level changes and is reachable from anywhere, such as score, settings, or music that must not restart.
Gives downsides of state that is reachable from anywhere: hidden dependencies, and values that any code can change.
Gives downsides for testing and start-up: harder isolated testing, and ordering and initialization problems.
Names two alternatives, such as passing data to the next scene during the switch, a data asset or resource shared by reference, saving to disk, or events that announce changes.
Gives a precise instruction that states what data is held, how long it lives (survives scene changes), who may change it and how others read it, instead of the word "global".

questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent "send my tester the game". The agent zips the project folder and reports that the task is done. Using the terms editor, running game and exported build, explain what is wrong with that, give three things that can differ between playing in the editor and playing a build, and write a precise instruction.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the editor (the tool the game is made in, including editor-only code), the running game (started from the editor or command line with the engine present) and an exported build (a standalone package for a target platform).
Explains that a zipped project folder is source material that needs the engine, and often an import step, to run, so it is not a build the tester can open.
Gives three real differences: editor-only code is absent, some files are excluded or filtered by export settings, and platform settings, performance or debug features differ from the editor run.
Names the step and its prerequisites: exporting in Godot (which needs export templates installed), building in Unity, packaging in Unreal, each for a chosen target platform.
Gives a precise instruction naming the target platform and configuration, the output location, and a check that launches the built artifact itself instead of the editor and reports the evidence.

questions.prompt: A developer who knows Unity starts working on a Godot project and later on an Unreal project. Give a mapping for at least six terms or ideas from Unity into Godot and Unreal terms (for example prefab, component, ScriptableObject, C# event, FixedUpdate and InputAction), and explain two places where the mapping is only approximate. Say why an agent told to "do it the Unity way" could build the wrong thing in the other engines.

rubric.text: Maps the template and instance idea correctly: Unity prefab, Godot scene instanced into another scene, Unreal Blueprint class with placed instances.

Maps the loops correctly: FixedUpdate to Godot's physics callback, Update to Godot's per-frame callback and to Unreal's per-frame Tick; saying that Unreal's default per-frame Tick has no direct equivalent of FixedUpdate, and that physics substepping or an optional asynchronous physics mode is the nearest, also earns the point.

Maps events, data assets and input correctly: C# event or UnityEvent to Godot signal to Unreal delegate or Event Dispatcher; ScriptableObject to Godot Resource to Unreal Data Asset; InputAction to a Godot Input Map action to an Enhanced Input action.

Explains at least two imperfect mappings, such as Godot nodes not behaving like Unity components, an Unreal Actor taking its transform from a root component, or a Godot scene doing the work of both a Unity scene and a prefab.
Explains the risk for an agent: a literal translation, such as adding components to a Godot node or creating a prefab file, builds something the target engine does not have or does not use.

questions.prompt: Explain Model Context Protocol to a game designer who thinks it is a cloud model that writes the game. Use an editor example to distinguish the host, client and server.

rubric.text: Defines MCP as an integration protocol connecting an AI application with external context and capabilities.
Identifies the host as the assistant application and the client as its protocol connector.
Identifies the server as the service exposing editor operations, with a concrete example such as inspecting a scene.
Separates language-model inference from tool execution and engine gameplay execution.
Explains that local or remote deployment is a configuration choice rather than a requirement to use cloud inference.

questions.prompt: Design an MCP interface for a hypothetical editor that must expose a scene inventory, a create-light operation and a reusable lighting-review checklist. Explain how the agent should use them together.

rubric.text: Maps the inventory to a readable resource with an identifier, or justifies a query tool when dynamic arguments are required.
Maps light creation to a tool with explicit target scene and meaningful parameters.
Maps the reusable checklist to a prompt template rather than claiming retrieval performs a review.
Describes reading scene context before deciding where and how to create a light.
Requires inspecting and testing the resulting lighting against stated criteria after the edit.

questions.source: Applied: define a safe tool contract
questions.prompt: Specify a hypothetical move-object tool for an agent. The editor contains several objects with the same display name. Describe the contract without relying on a particular engine API.

rubric.text: Requires an unambiguous object identifier and checks the intended project and scene.
Defines position units, coordinate space and whether the input is an offset or an absolute destination.
Specifies validation for missing objects and invalid or out-of-range values before mutation.
Returns structured evidence of the affected object and its resulting transform, with explicit failure information.
Describes a stale-state check or equivalent precondition plus a way to recover the prior transform.

questions.prompt: A tool call reaches an MCP server, but no object appears in the editor. Propose a diagnostic sequence that separates message delivery, argument validation, engine execution and verification.

rubric.text: Checks the matching request and response rather than inferring success from connection status.
Checks the advertised tool and argument contract, including identity, units and supported operation.
Inspects reported tool failure and relevant editor logs for execution errors.
Checks the correct project, scene and editor state, including whether the result exists but is hidden or unsaved.
Rereads the actual scene and records evidence before choosing a targeted repair or retry.

questions.prompt: A studio wants a cloud-hosted language model to help edit a Unity project on a workstation through a local MCP service. Describe the data flow and two separate boundaries the studio must manage.

rubric.text: Places model inference remotely while placing the editor and its MCP-facing integration locally.
Traces user intent through the host/client to an editor tool and the resulting observation back to the host.
Explains that project context sent to the remote model crosses a data-disclosure boundary.
Explains that invoking a local editing tool crosses an action/permission boundary distinct from remote inference.
Proposes concrete controls for both boundaries, such as context filtering and narrowly scoped local tools.

questions.prompt: An older editor MCP plugin works with one client but fails with another. Plan an investigation without assuming a particular protocol revision's initialization sequence.

rubric.text: Records client, plugin and supported protocol revisions for both working and failing combinations.
Consults the specification and vendor documentation applicable to those revisions.
Compares a minimal read-only trace to distinguish transport, discovery and capability mismatches.
Uses a documented compatible configuration or upgrade path and retests in an isolated project.
Records the resulting compatibility requirements and avoids inventing unsupported methods to force a connection.

questions.source: Advanced: stale context and concurrent editing
questions.prompt: A human and an agent are editing the same level. The agent plans changes from a scene inventory read several minutes earlier. Design a workflow that prevents overwriting the human's recent work.

rubric.text: Identifies the inventory as a potentially stale observation rather than a current authority.
Resolves object identities and compares relevant current state with the planning snapshot before mutation.
Uses an available revision precondition, lock or coordinated editing window to detect or avoid conflicting writes.
Applies a small bounded change and verifies its result without resetting unrelated edits.
On conflict, stops or replans from fresh state and preserves a recovery record rather than silently overwriting.

questions.prompt: Design a common agent workflow for placing checkpoints in Unity and Unreal. Explain what belongs in the shared layer and what must remain engine-specific.

rubric.text: Defines shared intent with observable requirements such as checkpoint count, locations and activation behavior.
Places discovery, planning, verification and failure reporting in a reusable workflow.
Keeps object creation, asset references and component configuration in engine-specific adapters.
Requires each adapter to expose its argument semantics and supported operations rather than reusing tool names blindly.
Verifies gameplay behavior independently in each engine and does not equate protocol compatibility with asset compatibility.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, 'Unity Spark is Unity's MCP, so installing an MCP server gives us Spark.' Correct the reasoning and propose a small evaluation of each workflow without assuming access to either product.

rubric.text: Describes Spark as a browser-based game-creation experience based on the supplied product distinction.
Describes an MCP integration as an interface exposing editor capabilities to a client.
Explains why installing an interface does not establish access to a separate product experience.
Proposes a bounded creation task with observable gameplay acceptance criteria for evaluating Spark if access is available.
Proposes discovery, a reversible editor edit and read-back verification for evaluating an installed MCP integration.

questions.prompt: A Unity team's vendor documentation replaces its older in-editor MCP server with a CLI-hosted server. Plan the migration while preserving project work. Do not give version numbers or menu paths.

rubric.text: Inventories the installed editor integration and client configuration to establish that the migration applies.
Creates a recoverable project/configuration checkpoint and selects a small test project.
Follows the replacement's documented setup and checks the actual advertised tool contracts.
Verifies project targeting, a read-only query and a reversible edit with persistence before switching normal work.
Records compatibility findings and a rollback route rather than treating the new connection as sufficient acceptance.

questions.source: Applied: say it to the Unity agent
questions.prompt: Write a precise instruction for a Unity agent to add three instances of an existing checkpoint prefab to a specified scene. The positions are world-space coordinates supplied by the designer. Existing prefab behavior must be preserved.

rubric.text: Identifies the project, destination scene and existing prefab asset without relying on display name alone.
Requires three distinct instances at the supplied world-space positions with coordinate units made explicit.
Preserves the prefab asset and existing instance behavior unless a stated requirement needs an approved change.
Requires checking instance count, transforms and checkpoint activation through normal gameplay interaction.
Requires saving and reopening the scene and reporting the changed assets plus actual validation evidence.

questions.prompt: A Unity script edit introduces a field, but the agent cannot set it through the editor bridge. The editor shows compilation errors and the old component layout. Explain a repair and verification sequence.

rubric.text: Treats compilation failure as a reason the edited script may not be loaded into the editor.
Reads the compiler diagnostics and fixes the relevant code or dependency issue without suppressing the error.
Waits for successful compilation/reload before inspecting the actual component layout.
Checks that the field belongs to the intended component and is exposed through the supported tool contract.
Sets the field, reads it back and tests the intended behavior rather than concluding from file contents alone.

questions.source: Applied: one lamp versus a prefab
questions.prompt: A Unity scene has twenty instances of a lamp prefab sharing a material. A designer wants one lamp blue. Explain how an agent should establish the edit scope, avoid unintended propagation and prove the result.

rubric.text: Identifies the requested lamp instance unambiguously.
Distinguishes an instance change from editing the prefab definition or shared material asset.
Chooses a justified per-instance material/property solution supported by the project's rendering setup.
Checks the requested lamp and representative unchanged lamps, including the shared asset's state.
Saves and reloads the intended changes and records any new asset or override for review.

questions.prompt: A Unity agent imports a mesh, creates a prefab and places instances. Import succeeds, prefab creation fails, and no instances have yet been created. Design recovery without rerunning the entire sequence blindly.

rubric.text: Records each step's actual result and identifies prefab creation as the first failed stage.
Inspects the imported asset and error details before choosing a targeted correction.
Reuses the verified import rather than generating duplicate assets on retry.
Creates and validates the prefab before placing instances, using stable identifiers or duplicate detection.
Verifies the final asset/instance counts and persistence while removing only artifacts known to belong to the failed attempt.

questions.prompt: An AI-assisted prototype looks impressive in a browser demo. Your team needs an accessible game with keyboard controls, a save system and a defined target platform. Specify an acceptance plan before adopting the prototype.

rubric.text: Turns the controls, accessibility behavior and save/load requirements into observable checks.
Verifies the available export/build workflow and tests the required target rather than inferring it from the browser demo.
Inspects asset provenance, dependencies and permissions relevant to the team's intended use without assuming generated means unrestricted.
Measures performance and functional behavior under a representative play session, including restart and save recovery.
Assesses whether the team can inspect, modify and maintain the delivered project and records unmet requirements.

questions.prompt: A team can expose either a general script evaluator or three narrow tools for inspecting lights, setting one light's intensity and saving a specified scene. Compare the designs for an automated lighting task.

rubric.text: Explains that a general evaluator is flexible but can perform much broader actions than lighting edits.
Shows how narrow tools validate project/object identity, allowed values and write scope.
Acknowledges that narrow tools may need extension when a legitimate operation is missing rather than inventing support.
Defines evidence such as old/new intensity, affected object identifiers and save results.
Chooses a justified design with independent validation and a recovery strategy for unexpected changes.

questions.source: Foundational: Unreal MCP and game AI
questions.prompt: Explain how an Unreal editor MCP server can help build an NPC without being that NPC's runtime intelligence. Give a plausible workflow and its limits.

rubric.text: Identifies the MCP server as an editor-facing integration exposing available operations.
Separates the assistant's development-time decisions from the NPC's packaged runtime behavior.
Describes creating or configuring the relevant Actor, components or gameplay logic through supported operations.
Requires compiling or validating the changed assets and testing the NPC during play.
Explains that an editor connection alone does not establish runtime behavior, packaged compatibility or production readiness.

questions.prompt: An Unreal MCP endpoint is reachable, but its expected scene toolset is absent. The integration uses separately enabled toolsets. Plan a diagnosis that avoids changing level content until the integration is understood.

rubric.text: Distinguishes successful transport communication from availability of the needed tool implementation.
Checks the enabled toolsets and applicable integration documentation.
Refreshes or rechecks the catalog using the integration's supported workflow.
Verifies the client targets the intended editor/project and uses a supported protocol configuration.
Runs a minimal read-only operation once available and records any unresolved capability gap instead of inventing a tool name.

questions.source: Applied: say it to the Unreal agent
questions.prompt: Write an instruction for an Unreal agent to place five existing checkpoint Blueprint Actors in a specified level. The designer supplies transforms and wants the Blueprint class left unchanged.

rubric.text: Identifies the project, level and Blueprint asset unambiguously.
Specifies five distinct instances with the supplied transforms and explicit coordinate semantics.
Limits edits to the placed instances and preserves the Blueprint class definition.
Requires count/transform inspection plus an activation test through representative gameplay interaction.
Requires saving the affected content, reopening it and reporting changed packages and validation results.

questions.prompt: A Blueprint door compiles, but it opens without a key and sometimes opens twice. Explain how to investigate the logic and verify a repair.

rubric.text: Distinguishes compilation success from correctness of the gameplay conditions.
Inspects the key check and event path, including possible duplicate bindings or repeated overlap events.
Uses a minimal reproduction with no-key and has-key cases and records the observed transitions.
Repairs the condition and guards repeated activation according to the intended door behavior.
Runs regression cases for no key, one valid activation and repeated interaction without weakening the requirements.

questions.prompt: An Unreal test tool returns a job identifier before the test finishes. Design an agent workflow that reports the pressure-plate test accurately and avoids launching duplicates.

rubric.text: Treats the initial result as accepted or running rather than passed.
Stores the job identifier and uses the tool's documented status/result mechanism.
Waits or polls within a bounded policy while keeping a distinction between running, failed, completed and unknown states.
Obtains the final assertions and diagnostics before claiming success.
On timeout or lost connection, checks the existing job before retrying and reports unresolved status honestly.

questions.prompt: An Unreal tool is replacing ten placeholder Actors with props. It replaces four, fails on the fifth and stops. Design recovery that preserves the original transforms and avoids duplicate props.

rubric.text: Records the identities and outcomes of the four completed replacements and the failed/remaining targets.
Inspects the failure and current scene state before changing anything else.
Uses recorded transforms and target identities to verify completed work and prevent duplicate replacement.
Chooses either a bounded resume or a rollback based on available recovery support, explaining the choice.
Verifies all ten final placements or the restored originals and reports any remaining partial state.

questions.prompt: An Unreal editor integration is documented for same-machine use with no remote authentication layer. A team wants to use it from a remote workstation. Explain why port forwarding is not a complete solution and propose a responsible evaluation.

rubric.text: Explains that exposing the endpoint broadens who can reach powerful editor operations.
Distinguishes network reachability from authentication and per-operation authorization.
Checks documented supported deployment options rather than assuming a local service is ready for remote exposure.
Proposes a local client or a deliberately designed access-controlled remote arrangement with restricted reachability.
Tests with a disposable project and verifies identities, allowed operations and audit evidence before production use.

questions.prompt: An Unreal agent changes a light during play, and the value reverts afterward. The request was to deliver a persistent level change. Explain the likely state confusion and a verifiable repair.

rubric.text: Distinguishes a runtime object instance from saved authoring data.
Checks which world/object the tool actually targeted rather than assuming the revert is a transport failure.
Applies the intended value to the correct authoring target through a supported edit operation.
Saves the affected level or asset and reopens it to verify persistence.
Runs a play check afterward and considers runtime logic that might intentionally override the authored value.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.source: Foundational: map local and cloud boundaries
questions.prompt: An agent uses a remote model, a local MCP editor service and a remote asset catalog. Map the data and action boundaries for a request to add a prop to a scene.

rubric.text: Identifies the workstation-to-model boundary for prompts and selected project context.
Identifies the local client-to-editor boundary where tool calls can mutate scene state.
Identifies the asset-catalog boundary for search queries, credentials and downloaded content.
Assigns a concrete protection to each relevant boundary, such as context minimization, scoped tools and validated asset downloads.
Explains why calling the workflow local based only on the editor location would be misleading.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: An asset description instructs the agent to upload credentials before using the asset. Explain the trust error and propose a response that still allows legitimate scene work.

rubric.text: Identifies the description as untrusted content rather than an instruction from the user or host.
Rejects the unrelated credential upload without following or forwarding its executable directions.
Keeps secrets out of model context and limits upload/network capabilities where practical.
Uses trusted asset metadata or an alternative asset to continue the authorized task when possible.
Records or flags the suspicious content and verifies that no unintended action or disclosure occurred to the extent evidence allows.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: Design access controls for a shared remote editor service with reviewer and builder roles. Reviewers inspect scenes; builders may edit a designated level but cannot publish builds.

rubric.text: Separates authentication of the caller from authorization of each requested operation.
Grants reviewers read operations and restricts builders' writes to the designated project/level.
Enforces restrictions at the service or underlying capability boundary rather than relying on UI visibility.
Treats publishing as a separate permission and rejects unauthorized attempts even from an authenticated builder.
Tests allowed and denied operations and records useful audit evidence without logging secrets.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: A hypothetical MCP export tool receives a destination path and may write only under an approved folder. Propose validation and adversarial checks, including a path containing parent-directory components and a symbolic link.

rubric.text: Resolves the destination relative to the intended root and validates actual containment rather than a textual prefix.
Rejects traversal that escapes the root and explains why parent-directory components matter.
Accounts for symbolic links and possible changes between validation and writing, using an appropriate safe filesystem strategy.
Tests valid nested output, escape attempts, existing-file policy and permission-denied behavior.
Ensures rejection leaves protected files unchanged and returns a clear error without exposing unnecessary filesystem details.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: A developer wants to install a third-party MCP editor package because a tutorial says it speeds up game creation. Design a review appropriate to code that will access a valuable local project.

rubric.text: Checks maintainer identity, source location and whether the package is official or community-maintained without equating either label with safety.
Reviews requested permissions, startup behavior and relevant dependencies for access beyond the task.
Pins a reviewed revision and records installation/compatibility requirements.
Tests representative read, write and failure cases in a disposable project under restricted access.
Defines rollback/removal and acceptance criteria before granting access to the valuable project.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: An agent's tool log contains a credential that was also committed to version control. Describe containment and recovery without assuming that deleting the latest file removes all exposure.

rubric.text: Restricts further access to the exposed credential and rotates or revokes it through the appropriate authority.
Identifies relevant copies such as history, logs and artifacts while avoiding further reproduction of the secret.
Moves legitimate credential use to an appropriate secret store or environment mechanism outside tracked content.
Reviews evidence of credential use and evaluates the affected scope rather than assuming no access occurred.
Adds redaction and a check against future secret inclusion, with cleanup coordinated so other work is preserved.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: A vendor says its editor integration runs locally. A studio requires no project data to leave its workstation. Describe how to evaluate the complete workflow before relying on that claim.

rubric.text: Distinguishes local tool execution from the location of model inference and context processing.
Inventories model endpoints, telemetry, update checks, asset services and other network dependencies.
Inspects configuration and tests observed network behavior in a controlled session with representative tasks.
Uses local inference and disables or constrains incompatible remote paths where supported, verifying the resulting workflow still works.
Documents remaining limitations and does not infer an offline guarantee from the local integration label alone.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.prompt: Design an audit record for an agent that changes game levels. It must support incident investigation and avoid becoming a store of sensitive project text and credentials.

rubric.text: Records operation identity, caller, target project/object, time or ordering information and correlation identifier.
Records outcome and bounded before/after evidence adequate to reconstruct relevant changes.
Redacts secrets and minimizes raw prompts, asset text and payload data that are not needed for the audit purpose.
Restricts log access and defines retention appropriate to the project.
Protects useful failure records from silent overwriting and tests that the trail can explain a representative partial failure.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.prompt: An agent claims a door interaction is complete after creating a script and taking a screenshot. Design a minimum evidence package for accepting a door that opens only when the player holds a key.

rubric.text: Requires inspecting the actual implementation and changed assets for the intended condition and scope.
Requires compilation/import validation without presenting it as behavioral proof.
Tests both the no-key rejection and has-key opening paths through representative interaction.
Checks persistence and the relevant play/build environment for the intended deliverable.
Reports actual outcomes and remaining limitations rather than relying on the completion claim or screenshot alone.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.prompt: An editor tool times out while creating a checkpoint. The operation has no documented atomicity guarantee. Explain how to recover without duplicating the checkpoint or deleting unrelated work.

rubric.text: Recognizes that a timeout leaves the execution outcome unknown.
Inspects the current scene and available operation records using a stable identifier or bounded search.
Uses a supported idempotency mechanism or explicit existence check before retrying creation.
Verifies exactly one intended checkpoint and its configured behavior after recovery.
Reports unresolved uncertainty if inspection is insufficient and avoids broad deletion or a false success claim.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.prompt: Write an engine-neutral specification for a checkpoint, then explain how Unity and Unreal implementations could satisfy it while using different object and scripting systems.

rubric.text: Defines activation, saved location and respawn behavior in observable terms independent of engine terminology.
Maps the Unity implementation to appropriate scene objects/components and a reusable asset where useful.
Maps the Unreal implementation to appropriate Actors/components and Blueprint or code behavior where useful.
Makes units, coordinate spaces, object identities and persistence explicit at each adapter boundary.
Uses equivalent gameplay acceptance cases in both engines without requiring identical tools or serialized assets.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.source: Applied: diagnose a flaky agent test
questions.prompt: An automated game test passes intermittently. It uses random spawn positions, rendered-frame waits and an asynchronously imported asset. Design a repeatable diagnosis and repair plan.

rubric.text: Records failures with seed, timing, import status and relevant engine configuration.
Controls or records random input so a failing spawn can be reproduced.
Uses a suitable fixed simulation step or bounded simulation-condition wait instead of assuming rendered frames equal elapsed game time.
Waits for successful asset readiness and distinguishes import failure from gameplay failure.
Reruns the repaired test under the controlled setup and retains failures rather than reporting only the first pass.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.source: Advanced: compare Unity and Unreal workflows
questions.prompt: A team wants an agent to import props, place them, configure collisions and run tests. Design a fair comparison of Unity and Unreal integrations without assuming that using MCP gives them identical capabilities.

rubric.text: Defines the same observable scene and gameplay requirements for both trials.
Inventories the actual tools, supported operations and required manual steps in each integration.
Measures task completion, correctness, recovery from a controlled failure and human effort on comparable inputs.
Includes team skills, target platform and engine-specific asset/workflow constraints in the decision.
Records compatibility and evidence limitations and chooses based on the measured task rather than tool count or a demo alone.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.prompt: An agent reduces a benchmark's steady frame time from 20 to 15 milliseconds for a 60 FPS target, but disables required shadows. Calculate the timing result and propose an acceptable next step.

rubric.text: Computes the target budget as about 16.67 milliseconds per frame and the baseline as 50 FPS.
Computes the new steady rate as about 66.67 FPS and the time saving as 5 milliseconds per frame.
Recognizes that the changed result meets the timing budget but violates the visual requirement.
Restores or preserves required shadows and profiles the actual bottleneck before choosing another optimization.
Rebenchmarks under the same workload and checks both timing variation and visual acceptance on the target environment.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.prompt: An agent writes a checkpoint feature and its test. The test directly assigns the expected saved position before asserting equality. Explain the weakness and design stronger evidence, including a negative case.

rubric.text: Identifies that the test sets its own expected outcome and bypasses the checkpoint behavior.
Drives the player through the actual activation path and then exercises respawn or load behavior.
Observes the resulting position independently of the setup assignment and uses a justified tolerance if needed.
Adds a negative case such as respawning before any checkpoint is activated or entering an inactive checkpoint.
Reviews the test against the requirement and checks that a deliberately broken activation path would be detected.

questions.section: Agent testing, troubleshooting and engine comparisons
questions.source: Advanced: recover a partial scene batch
questions.prompt: An agent changes five of ten lights before a tool fails. The contract does not provide transactions. Explain atomicity, design a recovery record and propose acceptance criteria for a resumed operation.

rubric.text: Defines atomicity as an all-or-nothing operation and explains why a batch call alone does not provide it.
Records per-light identity, original value, attempted value and observed outcome.
Inspects current state before choosing a bounded resume or restoration of verified prior values.
Avoids overwriting unrelated concurrent changes by checking preconditions or coordinating access.
Verifies all intended final values and unchanged out-of-scope objects, saves the result and reports any unresolved partial state.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: vague request rewrite
questions.prompt: A developer types this to a coding agent working in a game project: 'Add a score to my two-player paddle game and make sure everything still works.' Rewrite the request as a precise instruction, using the right terms for behaviour, constraints, checks and evidence, and include a new test for the score. Then explain at least three different things the agent could build or report wrongly because of the original wording.

rubric.text: States the required behaviour in observable terms (for example a point goes to a named player when the ball leaves through a named edge, and where both scores are displayed) instead of 'a score'.
Fences off what must not change (such as paddle movement, ball speed and bounce rules) and says which files not to edit; naming files to read first is optional.

Says exactly how the checks are run so that anyone can repeat them from the command line (for example headless, with the frame rate pinned, under a time limit, with exit code 0 as the pass condition), and asks for the real command output rather than a summary; any equivalent repeatable check that returns its evidence earns the point.

Requires a new test that exercises the real behaviour and checks observed state (for example by driving the game through its normal input events); a clearly labelled direct placement of the ball or paddles for setup is acceptable, but the score being asserted must not be written directly.
Names at least three ways the original wording could go wrong, such as 'works' meaning only 'it runs', a test weakened to pass, edits to unrelated behaviour, or a flaky run reported as a pass.

questions.source: Flaky tests and fixed frame rate
questions.prompt: A regression test for a game passes on one laptop and fails on another, and sometimes fails then passes on the same laptop with no change to the code. The test presses keys for a fixed number of frames. The game moves objects by speed times delta, where delta is the real time since the previous frame. Explain what 'flaky' means, why this test is flaky, and two different ways to make it deterministic. Say what you would check before concluding that the game code is at fault.

rubric.text: Defines a flaky test as one whose result varies with no change to the code or the test, and a deterministic test as one that gives the same result every run from the same code and inputs.
Explains the mismatch: the test counts frames, but the game advances by delta seconds, and frame duration depends on load and hardware, so the same frame count covers different amounts of game time.
Gives the first fix: run the engine with a fixed frame rate so every frame represents the same game time, whatever the machine does.
Gives the second fix: express the test in game seconds (hold the key for a stated amount of game time) instead of counting rendered frames.
Says what to check first: reproduce under the pinned configuration, change one variable at a time, repeat runs and compare recorded numbers.

questions.prompt: A coding agent reports 'Done, all tests pass.' For each of the following, say what it shows and what it does not show: the agent's report; a diff of the changes; a clean import and parse check; a passing automated headless test with the time step pinned; a person playing the game; a build running on the target platform. Then say which you would require before accepting the change and why.

rubric.text: Treats the agent's report as a claim that shows only that the agent produced a message, and says why the developer's own rerun is evidence.
Says a diff shows exactly which lines changed but not that the change works, and a clean import and parse check shows only that files load and scripts parse, not that behaviour is right.
Says a passing headless test with a pinned time step shows the tested state is right under that scripted input, while not covering look, feel, readability or unscripted inputs.
Says a person playing shows what one person experiences on one machine, and a build running on the target shows the game survives packaging, not that anyone wants to play it.
Names a justified minimum, for example reading the diff, rerunning the pinned test oneself and checking that no test was weakened, plus a human playtest for anything about feel.

questions.prompt: A developer wants a coding agent to import a game project and run its headless tests, but not to run arbitrary commands. Three options are on the table: (a) an allow rule for any command starting with the engine's program name; (b) allow rules for exact commands with fixed arguments; (c) running everything in a sandbox that can write only inside the project folder. Explain the difference between a permission grant and a sandbox, assess each option, and describe what the developer should still do personally.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the two: an allow rule decides which commands run without asking a human, while a sandbox technically limits what any running process can read, write or reach.
Judges (a) as wide: an engine that can run a script file can run whatever code that script contains, including starting other programs, so a program-name rule is not a boundary on behaviour.

Judges (b) as narrower and easier to reason about, while noting that an exact-match rule is narrow and may need updating when the command changes, and that rules should grant only what the developer can read and understand.

Judges (c) as limiting damage outside the folder but not inside it: the agent can still delete or overwrite project files and its own evidence, and legitimate writes outside the folder can fail with errors.
Says the developer should still read new commands and scripts before approving them, and review the diff before committing.

questions.prompt: A coding agent ran a project's regression test the wrong way, the test failed, and the agent gave a confident but wrong explanation. After the developer added a short section to a standing instruction file in the repository, the same request produced a correct run. Explain what 'context' means for an agent, why a standing instruction file helps, what that section should contain, and what it cannot do.

rubric.text: Defines context as the text available to the agent now (instructions, files it has read, command output), limited in size, with a new session starting without earlier conversations.
Explains that project-specific facts such as how to run tests, required flags and setup steps cannot be known unless written down, so the agent guesses and may produce a plausible but wrong run.

Lists what the section should contain: exact commands, required options (for example headless and a pinned frame rate), setup steps such as the import step, the expected result (exit code, expected numbers), a time limit, and which outputs to keep.
Says the file should also state what must stay a human decision or must not be edited.
Says a fluent explanation is not evidence and the instruction file does not guarantee identical design choices across runs, so the developer still verifies by their own run and reads the diff.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to verify, without opening a window, that a score label shows the correct number after the ball leaves the left edge of a game. Design the test: how it starts the game, how it drives it, what it reads, how it reports its result to a script, and how it guards against hanging. Then name two things this test cannot establish.

rubric.text: Loads the real game scene and drives it without shortcuts, either with the game's normal input events or by letting the real game play until the ball leaves, rather than writing the score or the ball's position directly.
Reads observable state: the score counter and the score label's text, compares them with the number of edge events it counted, and pins the time step so the run is repeatable.
Reports through the exit code (0 for pass, nonzero for fail) plus a readable report.
Guards against hanging by calling quit explicitly at the end and running the command under a time limit.

Names two limits, such as how the number actually looks when rendered (legibility, placement, overlap with other objects), how the game feels or whether the serve is fair, and behaviour under inputs or machines the test did not cover.

questions.source: Node, scene, instance and scene tree
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent working in Godot: "Spawn a bullet when the player fires." Define node, scene, instance and scene tree, and use them to describe what the agent has to do to make a bullet appear and move correctly. Explain what happens if the agent leaves out the step that puts the bullet into the scene tree, and what happens to the bullet's movement if the agent adds it as a child of the player rather than as a child of the level. Then write a more precise version of the instruction.

rubric.text: Defines the four terms accurately: a node is the basic building block with a type, a scene is a saved arrangement of nodes in a tree, an instance is a set of nodes created from a scene, and the scene tree is the live hierarchy of nodes in the running game.
Describes the steps: load the bullet scene as a packed scene, instantiate it to get a node tree, then add that tree as a child of a node that is already in the scene tree.
Explains that an instance that is never added to the tree does not appear or run: its callbacks such as _ready are not called and it is not part of the game.

Explains that a child inherits its parent's transform, so a bullet added under the player is carried along with the player and turns with it, whereas a bullet added under the level root moves in the level's space.
Gives a precise instruction that names the bullet scene, says to instance it on each shot, names the parent node to add it to, and says what position and direction to give it (in which space).

questions.prompt: In a Godot project, a coding agent wrote a coin script that, when the player touches the coin, runs get_parent().get_parent().add_score(10) to update the score display two levels up the tree. The same coin scene is reused in a new level that has a different tree layout, and the game now reports errors. Explain why the script broke, redesign it with a signal, and explain what the signal, the emit and the connection each do. State the usual advice about which direction calls and signals should go in a scene, and say what should happen when two sibling scenes need to cooperate.

rubric.text: Explains that the coin depends on the exact shape of the tree above it, so it only works where its ancestors happen to be arranged that way, and breaks when it is reused.
Redesigns it so the coin declares a signal (such as collected, with the value as an argument) and emits it when touched, without knowing who listens.

Explains that something above the coin (the level or the score display) connects a function to the signal, either in the editor or in code, and that emitting then calls the connected functions (immediately by default).
States the usual advice that parents call down into children they own and children announce upward with signals.
Explains that sibling scenes should not hold direct references to each other and that a shared ancestor should connect or mediate between them, which keeps each scene reusable.

questions.prompt: A coding agent produced this script for a Godot node: in _process it calls get_node("Label") to find a child, sets that child's text, and also moves the node with position.x += 5. It also loads a settings file from disk inside _process. The game runs 144 frames per second and the project's physics rate is 60 ticks per second. Explain what _ready, _process and _physics_process are each for and how many times each runs in 10 seconds in this setup, identify three problems in the agent's script, and say how to fix each.

rubric.text: Explains that _ready runs once when the node and its children have entered the scene tree, so one-time setup such as loading the settings file and finding children belongs there.
Gives the counts: about 1 call of _ready, about 1440 calls of _process (once per rendered frame) and about 600 calls of _physics_process (the fixed rate) in 10 seconds.
Identifies the repeated settings load and the repeated node lookup every frame as wasted work, and fixes them with a one-time load and an @onready reference or a lookup in _ready.

Identifies position.x += 5 per frame as frame-rate dependent (720 units per second at 144 frames per second), and fixes it by expressing the speed per second and multiplying by delta, or by using the fixed-step callback for physics-driven movement.
Explains why the fixed-step callback is chosen for physics bodies (a constant step independent of rendering) and the per-frame callback for visuals such as label text.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to tune enemy health, speed and damage without editing code, and several enemy types should share some base values. A coding agent has hard-coded the numbers in the enemy script. Explain what an exported variable is and what a custom Resource is in Godot, and design a setup that uses both. Describe one problem that appears when many enemies share one loaded resource and the game changes its fields while playing, and how to avoid it. Explain when in a node's start-up an exported value becomes available.

rubric.text: Explains that an exported variable is exposed to the editor so that each instance can carry its own value that can be edited in the Inspector without opening the script.
Explains that a custom Resource is a data container that extends the resource type and is saved as a file, so that several nodes or scenes can point at the same tuning data.
Designs the setup, for example a stats Resource with exported fields, saved per enemy type, with an exported slot of that type on the enemy so the designer chooses the file in the Inspector.

Describes the shared-state pitfall: loading the same resource gives every user the same in-memory copy, so changing health on it during play changes it for every enemy; the fix is to keep runtime state such as current health in the node, or to make a separate copy per enemy.
States that exported values are assigned after the object is created and its _init has run but before _ready, so _ready can read the designer's values while _init sees only the defaults.

questions.prompt: In a Godot game, players on a French AZERTY keyboard say that the WASD-style movement feels wrong, and clicking the Resume button on the pause menu also makes the character fire a shot. A coding agent had read the Space key and the W, A, S and D keys directly and handled the mouse in _input. Explain both bugs using the ideas of input actions, physical versus labelled keys, and the order in which input reaches nodes and the GUI. Describe the fix for each and write a precise instruction for the agent.

rubric.text: Explains that input actions in the Input Map name an intent and map it to bindings, so the code asks about the action and not about a particular key, and bindings can then be changed without editing code.

Explains the AZERTY problem: a binding by printed key label sends the movement keys to different physical positions on other layouts, whereas a binding by physical key position keeps the same hand shape, which is why physical keys suit WASD-style controls.
Explains the click-through bug: _input sees events before the GUI, so a click that the Resume button also uses is seen by the gameplay code as a shot.
Fixes it by handling gameplay events in _unhandled_input, which receives only events that no Control has consumed.
Writes a precise instruction that names the actions and their physical bindings, says to handle fire in _unhandled_input, and says what to test (a click on the button must not fire).

questions.prompt: A Godot game has three requirements: when an alarm rings every guard in the level must go on alert, the player's score must survive the move from the level scene to a game-over scene, and a door must open when its lock child has been picked. For each requirement choose between a group, an autoload and a signal, and justify the choice. Give one risk or limit of each mechanism, and for each requirement say what specific failure follows if the wrong mechanism is used (for example, if the score is kept in a script on a node of the level scene).

rubric.text: Chooses a group for the alarm: guards add themselves to a named group and one call on the scene tree calls the alert method on every member, so the alarm needs no list of references.

Chooses an autoload for the score: an autoload node is added under the root before the main scene and stays through scene changes, whereas data kept in a level node is freed with the level, so the score would read zero.
Chooses a signal for the door: the lock child emits a signal when picked and the parent connects to it, so the child does not depend on its parent's type.

Gives a risk or limit for each: group names are plain strings, so a misspelling silently matches nothing; an autoload is global state that hides dependencies and must not be freed at runtime; a signal does nothing until something is connected to it.
Explains that choosing the wrong mechanism costs a specific failure, such as a stale list of guards, a lost score, or a lock that only works inside one kind of parent.

questions.prompt: A coding agent summarised Godot behaviour in five claims. Evaluate each one as correct or incorrect and correct the wrong ones. (1) "_ready runs every time a node is added to the scene tree." (2) "Emitting a signal that nothing is connected to raises an error." (3) "An autoload is freed when the current scene is replaced and recreated for the next scene." (4) "queue_free() removes the node at the end of the current frame, so the node can still be used until then." (5) "@export var speed stores one speed value in the script, and every instance of the scene shares it."

rubric.text: Marks claim 1 incorrect: _ready is called once for each node, when the node and its children have entered the tree, and is called again only if it is requested again.
Marks claim 2 incorrect: emitting a signal with no connected functions is allowed and simply calls nothing.
Marks claim 3 incorrect: autoloads are children of the root that are loaded before the main scene and persist across scene changes, and they must not be freed at runtime.
Marks claim 4 correct: queue_free defers deletion to the end of the frame, so the node is still accessible until then.
Marks claim 5 incorrect: @export exposes the variable to the editor, and each instance of the scene can carry its own value, with the script supplying only the default.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: asset request rewrite
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent and an image generator: 'Make me a cool pixel-art enemy with a walk animation for my platformer, plus a jump sound and some background music that I can ship.' Rewrite this as a precise specification using the correct terms, and explain what would likely come back wrong from the original wording.

rubric.text: Fixes the on-screen size and viewport (for example 'reads as 32 pixels tall in a 640 x 360 game'), one facing direction and the view (side view), and a limited palette.
Specifies the animation layout: frame count, equal cells, the same scale and baseline in every frame, delivered as a sprite sheet PNG with an alpha channel rather than a baked background or a JPEG.

Separates the audio: a one-shot jump effect and a looping music track cut on a bar boundary with no fade-out, with the file kind and sample rate stated (lossless for the effect, compressed acceptable for long music).
Asks for a provenance record: the tool and version, the prompt and settings, the licence terms, any reference images with their licences, and the edits made.

Names concrete failures of the original wording, such as wrong size or perspective, no transparency, blurred or off-grid pixels, uneven frames, a non-looping track, or an asset that cannot legally ship.

questions.prompt: Pixel art looks crisp in an image viewer but smeared when it is enlarged in the running game. Explain the cause using the terms texture filtering (nearest and linear), scale and import settings. Say how you would fix it, what can still look wrong at some window sizes, and how you would check the result.

rubric.text: Explains that linear filtering blends neighbouring texels when a texture is enlarged, while nearest filtering takes the single closest texel so hard pixel edges survive.

Gives the fix as setting nearest filtering where the engine reads it (on the node or as the project default) and notes the difference in scope, rather than regenerating the art at a higher resolution.
Covers import settings: lossless compression for pixel art because lossy or hardware compression shows artifacts on small images, and mipmaps off unless the camera zooms far out.
Points out that a non-integer scale with nearest filtering gives uneven pixel widths (for example 2.5 times makes some pixels 2 and others 3 screen pixels wide) and that whole-number scales avoid it.
Describes a check in the running game at several window sizes and notes the source must really be on a pixel grid, since a smoothed or JPEG-compressed source cannot be fixed by filtering.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a sprite sheet, a texture atlas, a tileset and a tilemap: what each contains and what uses it. Then, for two situations (a walking character with eight frames, and a cave level built from forty reusable wall and floor pieces), say which of the four terms you would use in an instruction to a coding agent and what you would specify.

rubric.text: Defines a sprite sheet as one image holding animation frames, usually in equal cells of a grid, played in order to animate a sprite.
Defines a texture atlas as many separate images, often of different sizes, packed into one texture with a record of each rectangle, used mainly to cut texture switches and draw calls.
Defines a tileset as a library of reusable equal-sized tiles and a tilemap as the grid of level cells that each reference a tile from that library.
For the walking character, chooses a sprite sheet and specifies frame count, cell size, a shared baseline, alpha, and that playback speed is set in the engine.

For the cave, chooses a tileset painted into a tilemap, specifies tile size, tile types and matching edges, and explains that asking only for 'a tilemap' is ambiguous because it could return one fixed picture.

questions.prompt: A game needs a short coin-pickup sound, a looping ambient track and a three-minute music piece. For each, choose the kind of file and the playback behaviour you would specify to a coding agent, using the terms sample rate, lossless versus lossy, loop, one-shot, sound effect versus music and polyphony. Explain your choices and one way each could go wrong.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the roles: the coin is a short, event-triggered one-shot that may overlap itself, while the ambient track is a long loop and the music piece is long and streamed, either looping or played once as the answer states.
Chooses formats with reasons: uncompressed or lossless for short effects, a lossy file for long music to save space, optionally with a lossless master kept for re-export.
Explains sample rate as samples per second that limits the highest representable frequency to half the rate and raises file size when higher, and that it does not change loudness.

Specifies the ambient loop properly: matching start and end with loop points set so the join is not heard, no baked fade-out, and a listening check across the join; if the answer loops the music piece too, the same applies with a length that falls on a bar boundary, and a piece played once needs no loop point.
Handles rapid coin pickups: a single voice cuts off the earlier sound, so allow overlapping voices (polyphony) so quick pickups are all heard.

questions.prompt: A student ships a game with an AI-generated sprite that was made by giving the generator a reference picture whose source and licence were never recorded, and an AI-generated music track from a tool whose terms the student never read. Explain what 'provenance' means for a generated asset, why recording it matters, which risks the student has created, and what a good asset log contains.

rubric.text: Defines provenance as the documented origin and history of an asset: the tool and version, the prompt and settings, the date, the inputs and references, the edits and where it is used.
Gives reasons to record it: the asset can be reproduced or replaced, the person's own contribution (selection and edits) can be shown, and a problem can be traced after the fact.
Identifies the reference risk: an unknown-source picture can taint the result, and the uncertainty cannot be cleared unless the source is traced or the asset is replaced.
Identifies the terms risk: a tool's terms can restrict use (for example non-commercial limits or attribution duties), and ownership of purely generated output is not automatic and varies by country.
Lists a useful log entry: asset ID, tool or model and version, exact prompt and settings, references with their licences, the terms or a link, the edits made, the final file and where it is used.

questions.prompt: A developer wants a grass texture to cover a large ground surface using a 256 x 256 image. Explain what 'seamless' (tileable) means, how to check an image for it, why a seamless texture can still look wrong over a large area, and what to tell a coding agent so that the engine repeats it correctly.

rubric.text: Defines seamless as the opposite edges of the image matching, so copies placed side by side show no visible join, and notes this is a property of the image content that an engine setting cannot create.
Describes the check: lay copies side by side (for example 3 x 3) and look along the joins, since a single copy can look fine and still fail.

Explains visible repetition: distinctive features recurring at a regular spacing form a pattern even without a seam, and names a mitigation such as blending in variation, a second texture or larger source images.
Tells the agent to set the texture to repeat rather than clamp, and says what goes wrong otherwise (edge pixels stretch instead of the image repeating).
Tells the agent to state how many times the texture repeats across the surface (the tiling scale), so the 256 x 256 image is neither stretched over the whole ground nor repeated too finely.

questions.prompt: A game has background music, sound effects, spoken dialogue and interface clicks, and a settings menu with separate volume sliders for music and effects. Design the audio bus layout. Explain what a bus is, where each slider should act, what decibels measure, how you keep the mix from clipping, and what it means to duck the music under dialogue.

rubric.text: Defines a bus as a channel that audio is routed through before output, where volume and effects apply to every source routed to it, with a master bus at the end.
Proposes separate buses (for example Music, SFX, Dialogue, UI) feeding the master, and has each slider set the volume of its own bus so music and effects can be changed independently.
Explains decibels as a logarithmic, relative scale where 0 dB is no change and about 6 dB is a factor of two in amplitude.
Explains clipping: simultaneous sounds add, so the sum can pass the digital maximum and distort, and the master level is kept under it with headroom.
Defines ducking as automatically lowering the music bus while dialogue plays and restoring it afterwards so that speech stays intelligible.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: prop request rewrite
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: 'Make me a barrel in Blender and put it in my game so the player can bump into it.' Rewrite this as a precise instruction using the correct terms, and explain what could come back wrong from the original wording.

rubric.text: Gives the size in metres and the up axis (for example a stated height and width, with +Y up in the engine), so scale and orientation are not guessed.
Specifies the origin or pivot location (for example the centre of the base so the barrel stands on the floor at y = 0) and that scale and rotation are applied before export.
States a triangle budget, the material count and names, and the export format (for example .glb) with the settings that matter.
Specifies the collision: a simple separate shape (primitive or convex) with its size, and says whether the barrel is static or moving, rather than 'collision' in general.
Lists concrete failures of the original wording, such as the wrong size, lying on its side, sinking into the floor or an expensive or missing collider.

questions.prompt: A model looks right in the modelling tool but arrives in Godot too large, lying on its side, rotating about the wrong point, or carrying an odd scale. Explain, using the terms units, up axis, origin (pivot) and applying transforms, what can cause each symptom and what number you would check to confirm each cause. Also say why looking at the model on screen is not enough to catch these problems.

rubric.text: Too large or too small: the engine reads 1 unit as 1 metre while the model was built in other units; checks the bounding box size in metres against the intended size.
Lying on its side: the modelling tool's up axis (Z) differs from the engine's (Y) and the export did not convert; checks which axis carries the height in the imported bounding box.

Odd scale: the object's scale was never applied, so the mesh data is a different size from what it looks like and the node carries a non-unit scale; checks the node scale is (1, 1, 1) and the mesh size is correct.
Rotating about the wrong point: the origin is not where the use needs it, such as at a hinge; checks the hinge position relative to the origin.
Explains why a model can look right on screen while one of these numbers is wrong, so the numbers must be measured and not only looked at.

questions.prompt: A level in a Godot project contains a stone archway the player walks through, a rock the player cannot move, and a crate the player can push. For each, choose a collision shape and justify it using the terms convex, concave (trimesh), primitive shape, static body and moving body. Explain what goes wrong if the agent is simply told to 'use the mesh as collision'.

rubric.text: Defines convex (no dents or holes; every line between two inside points stays inside) and concave or trimesh (follows the mesh triangles exactly), and primitive shapes such as box, sphere and capsule.
Chooses a concave or several convex pieces for the archway so the opening stays passable, noting a single convex hull would fill the opening and block the player.

Chooses a shape for the immovable rock with a stated reason: a concave shape is acceptable because the body is static, though a convex hull or a primitive is cheaper and equally adequate; and notes that in Godot concave shapes are usable only on static bodies and are the slowest option.
Chooses a primitive or convex shape for the pushable crate, since a moving body cannot use a trimesh in Godot and simple shapes are cheaper.

Explains what 'use the mesh as collision' risks: an expensive trimesh on a moving body that the engine may not support or that wastes processing, a hull that blocks the archway, or fussy detail that catches the player, and that collision geometry is a separate, simpler design choice from the visual mesh.

questions.prompt: A coding agent can drive Blender in two ways: through an MCP server connected to an open Blender window, or by writing a Python script that uses bpy and running Blender without a window. Explain what an MCP server lets an agent do, compare the two approaches, and say which you would choose for making a prop that must be regenerated later and why. Include one safety concern.

rubric.text: Explains that an MCP server exposes tools the agent can discover and call, with the server relaying calls to the target application and returning results, while the model itself stays outside.
Explains that bpy is Blender's Python API and that a script run in background mode builds and exports an asset with no window.
Compares them: MCP suits exploring a scene or one-off fixes and leaves a transcript of calls, while a script is a file that can be reviewed, diffed and rerun to regenerate the asset.
Chooses the script for a prop that must be regenerated, because the recipe is a file that can be rerun to give the same asset.

Names a safety concern, such as tools that run generated code in Blender without guards, a connection that anyone who can reach it can use, or remote generation services that cost money, and says to keep it local and approved.

questions.prompt: A scene has 50 trees, each a 12,000-triangle mesh with two materials. Explain the parts of a mesh (vertex, edge, face, triangle), how triangle count is worked out, why the vertex count a profiler reports can be higher than the count in the modelling tool, and how level of detail (LOD) and fewer materials reduce cost. Give the arithmetic for one example.

rubric.text: Defines vertex (point), edge (line between two vertices) and face (surface bounded by edges), and says GPUs draw triangles, with an n-sided face giving n - 2 triangles.
Works out a triangle count correctly for an example, such as a box having 6 quads and so 12 triangles, or the 50 trees totalling 600,000 triangles.
Explains that vertices are duplicated on the GPU where normals or UVs differ, as at a hard edge or UV seam, so a cube's 8 vertices can appear as 24.

Explains LOD as several versions of decreasing triangle counts chosen by distance, so far objects cost fewer triangles; a second calculation is not required, but one such as 40 distant trees at 1,500 triangles costing 60,000 instead of 480,000 earns the point.
Explains that each additional material typically adds at least one draw call, so merging materials where the look allows it reduces draw calls even when triangle count is unchanged.

questions.source: Diagnosing normals, UVs and material slots
questions.prompt: Three symptoms appear on imported models: some faces are black or invisible from outside; a texture looks stretched or is missing; and one object has far more draw calls than expected. Explain, using the terms normals, UV map and material slot, what each term means, which symptom each most likely causes, and how you would phrase the fix to a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines normals as direction vectors perpendicular to the surface used for lighting and culling, and links black or vanishing faces to inward-pointing normals.
Phrases the fix for normals precisely, for example 'recalculate the normals so they point outward', rather than 'fix the shading'.
Defines a UV map as the per-vertex 2D coordinates linking surface to image, and links missing or stretched textures to absent or poorly laid-out UVs, fixed by unwrapping.
Defines a material slot as a position holding a material to which faces are assigned, and links many draw calls to many slots or materials on one object.
