Gives a precise fix phrase for the slot problem (for example reduce the object to a stated number of materials, merging slots that share a look).

questions.prompt: An agent reports that an exported prop 'looks right'. Design a short list of measurements, taken after import into the engine and run headless, that would check the prop is the intended size, orientation, scale, pivot, materials and collision. For each check say what number you read and what failure it would catch, then say what a headless check cannot establish.

rubric.text: Checks size and orientation by reading the bounding box in metres and comparing it with the intended extents, catching wrong units or a prop lying on its side.
Checks scale by confirming the node scale is (1, 1, 1) and the mesh itself has the right size, catching unapplied transforms.
Checks the pivot by reading the lowest point relative to the origin (for example zero at the base), catching a prop that sinks or floats.
Checks materials by listing the material names or count on the imported surfaces, and collision by reading the shape type and size and confirming it is simple and sits where expected.
States what remains for a person: how it looks under the game's lighting, whether it reads as intended, whether the collider feels fair, and anything in the render that numbers cannot show.

questions.source: Collider versus trigger, say it to the agent
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction for a 2D Godot game: "Add a collider to the shield pickup so that the player can collide with it and get the shield." Explain the two different things the word "collide" could mean here, what the agent could build wrongly, and then rewrite the instruction precisely using the terms collider, trigger (area), layer and mask. State one observable result that would show the pickup works.

rubric.text: Distinguishes a solid collider, which blocks or deflects other bodies and produces a collision response, from a trigger or area, which only reports that an overlap began or ended and blocks nothing, and identifies that the pickup should be the detection kind the player can walk through (a Godot Area2D, a Unity trigger collider, or an Unreal overlap), not a solid obstacle.
Names a plausible wrong build: a solid body that stops or pushes the player so it cannot be collected, or a detection region whose layer and mask never see the player so nothing fires.

The rewrite specifies a detection-only region with its own collision shape, an event on the player's entry that gives the player the shield (removing the pickup afterwards is optional), and an explicit statement that it must not block movement.
The rewrite assigns the pickup its own layer and sets the scanning side's mask so that only the player is detected.
States one observable result that shows the pickup works, such as the player passing through the pickup and the shield state being set once.

questions.prompt: A teammate says "collider, trigger and raycast are all just ways of finding out that two things touched". Write a correction. For each of the three, say what it is, what it does and does not do, and give one gameplay use. Then name the corresponding term for the trigger in Godot, Unity and Unreal, and state one rule for choosing between them when briefing a coding agent.

rubric.text: A collider is a solid shape whose contacts produce a collision response (blocking, sliding, pushing); it does not merely report.

A trigger is a non-blocking region that reports entering and leaving to code (and staying, by asking which objects are inside now or through a stay event in engines that have one); it applies no response.

A raycast is a query along a line that returns the first thing hit (or nothing) at that moment; it is not a physical body (it may be run through a node or a direct physics query, but it is a question, not an obstacle), has no width, and does not block, push or notify anything.

Half a point if all three uses are fitting, such as a wall or floor (collider), a pickup or damage zone (trigger), and line of sight or a hitscan shot (raycast); half a point for naming the trigger's engine terms: Godot Area, Unity trigger collider, Unreal overlap.

States a sound selection rule, such as: if it must stop things use a solid collider, if it must notify when something is inside use a trigger, if it must ask a question about the space along a line use a raycast, and the brief should say which.

questions.prompt: A 2D game has walls, a player, enemies, player bullets, enemy bullets and coins. The design requires: the player is blocked by walls; enemies are blocked by walls but pass through one another; player bullets hit enemies but not the player or coins; enemy bullets hit the player; coins are detected only by the player. Design the collision layers and masks, explain the difference between a layer and a mask, and explain why writing the numbers into code needs care. Assume Godot, and say why leaving every object on the default layer would be unsuitable.

rubric.text: Defines a layer as the layer or layers an object appears in, and a mask as the layers it scans for contacts; detection runs from the scanner's mask to the other object's layer.

Gives every type that another object must scan or ignore its own layer (for example walls, player, enemies and coins, with bullets on one shared layer or split into player and enemy bullets) rather than leaving everything on the engine's default layer.

Sets masks that satisfy the five rules, for example enemies scan walls but not the enemy layer, player bullets scan enemies only, enemy bullets scan the player, and coins are detected only by the player: either the player (or its pickup area) scans the coin layer, or the coin's detector scans the player's layer, and either direction is accepted if no other object can detect coins (the rules do not require enemies and the player to collide, so a design may include or omit that contact).
Explains why the default is unsuitable: with everything on one layer and scanning that layer, everything collides with everything, which is why explicit settings are needed.

Explains that in code layers are bitmask integers, so layer n has the value 2 to the power n minus 1 (layer 3 is 4), so a layer number written as a bit value selects the wrong layer; functions that take layer numbers avoid this.

questions.prompt: A jump written in the per-frame update callback reaches a slightly different height on a 30 frames-per-second machine than on a 144 frames-per-second machine, and fast objects sometimes pass through thin walls. Explain what a fixed time step is, why physics and collision movement belong in the fixed-step callback (Godot's _physics_process, Unity's FixedUpdate), and what goes wrong with a variable step. Finish with one precise sentence you would give a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines a fixed time step: the physics simulation advances in equal increments of game time (for example 1/60 s) regardless of how often frames are drawn.
Explains that the per-frame callback runs at a variable rate, and that the engine may run zero, one or several physics steps per rendered frame to keep the physics clock steady.
Explains the consequence of a variable step: integration with different step sizes gives different jump arcs and contact results, so behaviour depends on frame rate.
Explains that long steps let fast bodies move farther than a thin obstacle is thick and so skip it (tunnelling), and that a constant step makes behaviour reproducible and testable.
Gives a precise instruction naming the callback, such as "apply gravity and call the character body's movement function only inside the physics-process callback, and use the physics step's delta".

questions.prompt: In a game whose physics runs at 60 steps per second, a bullet (a RigidBody2D with a circular collider 6 px across) travels at 900 px/s toward a wall that is 8 px thick. Continuous collision detection is off. The bullet usually stops at the wall but occasionally passes through it. Use arithmetic to explain why, define tunnelling and continuous collision detection, and compare three remedies with one cost each.

rubric.text: Computes the step distance, 900 / 60 = 15 px per physics step.

Shows the arithmetic that makes a miss possible: the bullet overlaps the wall only while its centre is within 8 + 6 = 14 px of range, which is smaller than the 15 px spacing between tested positions, so some bullets land on both sides without ever overlapping.

Defines tunnelling as a fast body passing through a thin obstacle because overlap is tested only at discrete positions, and explains it happens only for some bullets because it depends on where the tested positions fall relative to the wall.
Defines continuous collision detection as testing the path swept during a step instead of only the end position, and notes it costs more per body, so it is turned on for fast, small bodies.

Compares remedies with a cost for each, such as continuous collision detection (cost per body), a raycast from the previous to the new position or a hitscan design (more code, no physical bullet), and thicker walls or a higher physics rate (art constraint or global cost).

questions.source: Static, kinematic, dynamic and character bodies
questions.prompt: A developer must brief a coding agent on a 2D platformer. For each of these, choose a body type (static body, kinematic body, dynamic or rigid body, character body, or trigger region) and justify the choice, saying whether it blocks: the level floor, an elevator platform moved by code, the player, a pushable crate, a spike strip that hurts on contact, and a health pickup. Give Godot and Unity names where you can.

rubric.text: Explains the distinction in terms of who moves the object: static is never moved, kinematic is moved by code or animation, dynamic is moved by the physics simulation, and a character body is moved by code with collision detection and no simulation.

Assigns the floor to a static body (Godot StaticBody2D, Unity static collider) that blocks, and the elevator to a kinematic body moved by code or animation (Godot AnimatableBody2D, Unity kinematic Rigidbody) that blocks and, when moved, affects other bodies in its path (pushing them or carrying a body that stands on it).
Assigns the player to a character body (Godot CharacterBody2D, with gravity and jump written in code) and the crate to a dynamic body (Godot RigidBody2D) that the simulation pushes and moves.
Assigns the health pickup to a trigger region (Godot Area2D, Unity trigger collider) that detects the player and does not block.

Handles the spikes sensibly, either as a detection region or hitbox that reports contact and does not block, or as a solid spike block that also damages (a static body plus a damage region); either choice earns the point if the answer says which and whether it blocks.

questions.prompt: A melee game needs a sword attack. Design the collision setup using the terms hitbox, hurtbox and body collider. Say which of the three are solid and which are detection regions, how layers and masks keep the player from hitting themselves, when the hitbox should be active, how to make sure each enemy is damaged at most once per swing, and give the one-paragraph instruction you would give the coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines the three terms: in the melee convention the hitbox deals damage during an attack and the hurtbox receives it (the reverse naming used in shooters is accepted if it is stated and applied consistently), and the body collider is the solid shape that blocks movement.
States that the body collider is solid while the hitbox and hurtbox are detection regions (areas or triggers) that report overlap and do not block.

Uses layers and masks so the sword's hitbox scans the enemies' hurtbox layer and not the player's own; the hurtbox may be on a layer separate from the body collider, or share one layer if the answer states how double hits are prevented.
Activates the hitbox only for the damaging frames of the swing, and records which targets were already hit in this swing so each is damaged at most once.

The agent instruction is precise: it names the three shapes, their layers and masks, the active frames, the once-per-swing rule, and one checkable result such as an enemy losing exactly the damage amount a single time.

questions.prompt: A developer asks a coding agent for three behaviours: a crate knocked away by an explosion, a rocket that accelerates while its engine burns, and a character that moves left or right at 200 px/s while a key is held. For each, choose force, impulse or setting velocity, and body type, and justify. Explain why applying an impulse from a per-frame callback is a bug.

rubric.text: Defines the terms: a force acts over time and produces acceleration, an impulse is an instantaneous change in momentum applied once, and velocity is the current speed with direction, which can be set directly.

Models the explosion knock-back as one impulse on a dynamic (rigid) body (optionally noting that the same impulse changes a heavier body's velocity less, since change in velocity is impulse divided by mass).
Models the rocket's thrust as a force applied on every physics step while the engine burns, giving steady acceleration until drag or collision intervenes.

Moves the character by setting its velocity, and says who owns the motion: a character body (Godot CharacterBody2D with move_and_slide) fits because it is not simulated and the code owns its motion; a kinematic body, or a rigid body whose linear velocity is set directly, is also accepted if the answer justifies it.

Explains that an impulse applied once per rendered frame is applied a different number of times per second on different machines, so the total push depends on the frame rate; continuous effects belong in forces in the fixed-step callback.

questions.prompt: A game gives the player a 3-second invulnerability power-up. Enemy damage is applied in a handler connected to the "body entered" signal of the player's detection area. In testing, an enemy that is already overlapping the player when the invulnerability ends does not hurt the player until it leaves and re-enters. Explain the cause in terms of enter events versus the set of current overlaps, propose two fixes, and describe a test that would catch the bug.

rubric.text: Explains that an enter event fires once when an overlap begins, and nothing new begins when the invulnerability ends, so an overlap that started earlier stays unreported.
Distinguishes an event (a change) from a query (the current state): the engine can be asked which bodies overlap now.
Proposes a first fix: when the invulnerability ends, query the current overlapping bodies and apply damage to any enemy found.
Proposes a second fix, such as polling the overlap list every physics step for damage logic, or using a stay event where the engine has one, so damage does not depend on a one-time entry.

Describes a deterministic test: place an enemy overlapping the player, let the power-up expire at a fixed frame rate, and assert damage within a stated number of physics steps, noting a casual playtest could miss the case.

questions.prompt: A designer hands a coding agent this requirement: "The checkpoint should feel responsive and reset the player quickly." Explain why a stranger could not test it, then rewrite it as acceptance criteria that a person who has never met the designer could turn into tests. Your criteria must show how you handle quantities, tolerances, time, how each state is reached, and what must not change.

rubric.text: Identifies the untestable words ("feel responsive", "quickly") and explains that they are judgements without a quantity, so two testers could disagree about pass or fail.
Names quantities with units and a tolerance, for example a respawn position within 0.2 m or 8 px of a named marker.

Gives time as a stated limit with a stated basis, for example within 2 physics ticks, 120 frames at a stated fixed rate, or 0.5 seconds at a stated tick rate (a game-clock basis is one example), not "quickly".
States how each state is reached: by real input actions or by a clearly labelled direct write of game state.
Lists what must not change, such as existing behaviour and the existing tests, which must still pass.

questions.prompt: A developer writes this instruction to a coding agent: "Create a boolean called shielded and a Timer node called ShieldTimer set to 3.0 seconds, and connect the pickup's area_entered signal in code." The designer actually cares that the player is protected for three seconds after collecting a pickup. Distinguish a specification from an implementation, explain what is wrong with the instruction as written, and rewrite it as a specification that is measurable and covers at least one edge case. Say when an implementation constraint is legitimate.

rubric.text: Defines a specification as the observable behaviour that must hold, and an implementation as the mechanism chosen to achieve it (nodes, variables, signals).

Explains what is wrong: the instruction fixes names and mechanisms but never states the behaviour the designer wants, so a build that follows it can still be wrong, and a test cannot be written from it.
Rewrites as behaviour: after collecting a pickup, enemy contact deals no damage for 3.0 s, and after 3.0 s contact damages again.

Makes the 3.0 s measurable (a tolerance or a tick count) and states an explicit rule for at least one edge case, such as a second pickup during the window (restart, extend or ignore are all acceptable if stated) or expiry while an enemy overlaps.

Names a legitimate implementation constraint, such as an architectural rule the project already follows, a file the agent may edit, or something that must not change, and says these belong beside the behaviour, not in place of it.

questions.prompt: A studio pitches a 2D stealth puzzle game with thirty levels. Define a prototype, a vertical slice and a minimum viable product (MVP), say what each would contain for this game, and say what question each build is meant to answer. Then explain how confusing them leads to scope problems.

rubric.text: Defines a prototype as a quick build that tests one design question, with placeholder art, which may be thrown away.
Defines a vertical slice as a thin portion of the game built to near-final quality across art, audio, UI and mechanics, to show the whole game can reach that standard.
Defines an MVP as the smallest complete game that can be released and tested with real players, containing only the features it needs.

Applies each build to the stealth game with concrete content (for example: one room with a guard and hiding; one finished level with final art and sound; a handful of levels with menus and saving) and states the question each answers (is it fun, can we build the whole to this standard, will players want it); full point for content and a question for all three builds, half a point if two of the three are covered.
Explains a scope problem from confusion, such as polishing a prototype, treating the slice as the product, or adding roadmap features to the MVP, which grows scope and delays learning.

questions.prompt: Three weeks before a deadline, a team's design pillars are "tight controls", "readable levels" and "short sessions", and its scope list has twelve levels. Teammates propose online leaderboards, a branching story with cutscenes, and procedurally generated levels. Explain scope and scope creep, show how pillars and an out-of-scope list help the team decide, and describe the options and records a good lead would use.

rubric.text: Defines scope as the commitment of features and content for a date, and scope creep as growth of that commitment without matching changes in time or resources.

Uses the pillars as filters, giving a verdict for each of the three proposals and arguing it from a pillar (for example the branching story with cutscenes conflicts with "short sessions" and the generated levels risk "readable levels"); any verdict is accepted if it is argued from a pillar or from cost.
Names the levers available: cut, defer, swap one feature for another of equal cost, or move the date, and explains that accepting without trade is creep.
Explains that an out-of-scope list records decisions already made so they are not re-argued, and that each proposal gets an estimate of cost before a decision.
Describes recording the decision and reason, so that a rejected idea becomes a post-release candidate rather than a lost argument.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a stealth meter that fills while an enemy can see the player. Using mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, trace what the designer builds and what emerges, explain why the designer cannot set the aesthetic directly, and show how to turn the mechanic into a precise requirement a coding agent can build and a test can check.

rubric.text: Defines mechanics as rules and systems the designer builds, dynamics as behaviour that emerges when players use them, and aesthetics as the emotional responses of players.
Identifies the meter and its fill rule as the mechanic, and gives plausible dynamics such as players hugging cover, waiting for patrol gaps, or rushing between blind spots.

Identifies aesthetics such as tension and the satisfaction of slipping past, and explains why the designer cannot set them directly: they are the players' own responses, so the designer can only shape the rules that tend to produce them.
Explains that a playtest is needed to find which dynamics and feelings a rule produces, because they cannot be read from the rule.
Writes the mechanic as numbers and observable results, such as fill rate per second while seen, decay rate when unseen, the threshold at which enemies attack, and a test that checks these values.

questions.prompt: A coding agent reports that a new level is finished and all its tests pass. Explain what passing automated tests can and cannot establish about the level, what a playtest can show that a test cannot, and design a verification plan with three automated criteria and two playtest questions. Include one way to check that the tests would actually fail if the level were broken.

rubric.text: States that passing tests establish only the specific conditions they check, such as reachability, counts or timings, and not whether the level is fun, readable or fair.
Explains that a playtest with real players can show whether they understand what to do, notice cues and enjoy the level, which no automated test decides.

Gives three testable automated criteria with quantities, tolerances or time boxes, for example that the exit is reachable by ordinary input within a set number of frames and that the hazard count and positions match the specification.
Gives two playtest questions, such as where players hesitate or fail repeatedly, and whether they can say what the goal was without being told.
Describes a way to check the tests are meaningful, such as breaking the level on purpose (blocking the exit or changing a value) and confirming that the test fails.

questions.prompt: In an interview for a graphics or technical-art role you are asked: "What is a fragment?" Answer as you would to a colleague who must give a coding agent precise instructions. Define the term, say how a fragment differs from a pixel and from a vertex, and use a concrete example with numbers (for instance a quad with four vertices, or two overlapping triangles) to show how many of each exist. Then explain one way a developer's instruction to a coding agent would change if the developer confused these terms.

rubric.text: Defines a fragment as the candidate produced by rasterization for each screen position a triangle covers, carrying interpolated values (such as UV, colour and depth), and the unit on which the fragment (pixel) shader runs.

Distinguishes it from a pixel: a pixel is the final element of the output image, several fragments can compete for one pixel (overdraw), and a fragment only becomes the pixel's colour if it survives the depth and stencil tests and discard, and its colour is then combined with the framebuffer by blending.
Distinguishes it from a vertex: a vertex is a corner point with attributes (position, UV, colour) handled by the vertex shader, and fragment values are interpolated from the vertices.

Gives a consistent numeric example, for example four vertices but 4096 fragments for a quad covering 64 × 64 pixels, or 300 plus 100 fragments for overlapping triangles, showing that fragment count follows screen coverage while vertex count follows the mesh.

Connects the distinction to instructions: per-pixel colour effects (flash, tint, dissolve) are fragment-stage work, shape or position changes are vertex-stage work, and mixing them up sends the agent to edit the wrong stage.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: precise wording for an effect
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: "Add a shader to the player so it looks hurt." The player is a multi-coloured 2D sprite with transparent areas around the artwork. Rewrite this instruction precisely, using the correct shader terms, so that the agent can build exactly one thing (choose one hurt effect, such as a red tint that fades out). Then explain at least three different wrong things the agent could have built from the vague version, and why each is wrong.

rubric.text: The rewritten instruction names the shader kind (a 2D sprite shader, such as Godot's canvas_item shader, or the equivalent unlit 2D shader in another engine) and the stage (fragment), because the change is to colour, not to geometry.

It specifies the control: a float uniform from 0 to 1 and, for a tint, a target colour written in RGBA components from 0 to 1, with the output colour mixed toward the target by that amount (any other single, fully specified effect is accepted).
It states that alpha must be preserved so transparent texels stay transparent, and that at 0 the sprite looks exactly as before.

It says who drives the effect: game code sets a uniform at the moment of the hit, either a progress value that returns to 0 over a duration in seconds or a hit time that the shader compares with engine time, rather than relying on a bare global clock or a frame count.

It names at least three plausible wrong builds and why they fail, for example a vertex shader that wobbles the mesh, a colour multiplier that cannot reach the target colour, a permanent tint, opaque output that fills the transparent area with a box, or a shared material that tints every sprite.

questions.prompt: For each of these four requests, decide whether the main work belongs in the vertex stage or the fragment stage, and justify the choice: (a) a flag waving on a mesh with many vertices, (b) an enemy dissolving into holes that follow a noise pattern, (c) a character squashing and stretching when it lands, (d) horizontal scanlines drawn over the whole screen. Explain what data flows from the vertex stage to the fragment stage, and why the cost of each stage differs for a large on-screen object.

rubric.text: Waving flag: vertex stage, because it displaces vertex positions; it is only as detailed as the vertex count, so a coarse mesh would need subdividing or a fragment-stage distortion of the sampling coordinate instead.
Dissolve: fragment stage, because the keep-or-discard decision is made per pixel by comparing a noise sample with a threshold, which a per-vertex stage cannot do.
Squash and stretch: vertex stage (or an object transform), because it changes the shape of the geometry rather than the colour of pixels.
Scanlines: fragment stage using the pixel's screen-space position, because the pattern must vary per output pixel independent of the mesh's own UV.

Half a point for explaining the data flow: the vertex stage runs once per vertex and passes interpolated values (varyings such as UV) onward; half a point for the cost: the fragment stage runs once per covered pixel, so for a large object fragment work greatly outnumbers vertex work.

questions.prompt: A game needs four visuals: a chain-link fence, a ghost, a window pane in a building, and an enemy that dissolves away. Explain the difference between alpha blending and alpha testing (discard), and choose the better technique for each visual. Include how each technique behaves with draw order, what the edges look like, and one cost or limitation of each. Support the draw-order point with a small calculation or example.

rubric.text: Defines alpha blending: the new fragment's colour is mixed with what is already in the framebuffer according to alpha (new × α + old × (1 − α)), allowing partial transparency.
Defines alpha testing or discard: a fragment is kept or dropped by comparing alpha (or a noise value) with a threshold, with no in-between opacity, so edges are hard and may look jagged.

Explains draw order: blending is order-dependent (a short calculation such as red over blue then green differing from green over blue then red), so translucent objects are normally sorted far to near, while alpha-tested fragments need no sorting.

Matches the visuals sensibly: fence (alpha test), ghost and window glass (blending, since they need partial transparency), dissolve (discard against a noise threshold, possibly with a blended soft edge).
States a cost or limitation of each: blending adds overdraw and sorting problems; discard has a performance cost on some GPUs because it can defeat depth optimisations.

questions.prompt: A developer asks a coding agent for a "damage pulse": when a sprite takes a hit, a red tint should appear at full strength and fade to nothing over 0.4 seconds. The agent first writes a shader that uses the engine's global time value as its clock and then a version where a counter lowers a value by a fixed amount each rendered frame. Explain why both designs fail, and design a correct one. Cover what a uniform is, who sets it, how the duration stays the same at 30 and 144 frames per second, and what happens if several sprites (for example enemies) that share one material are hit at different times.

rubric.text: Defines a uniform as a value set from outside the shader (game code), identical for all invocations of a draw, and says it is the contract through which game events reach the shader.
Explains why global engine time fails for an event-triggered effect: it counts from engine start, not from the hit, so the effect would play once at startup or at an arbitrary phase.
Explains why a per-frame decrement fails: the duration is a number of frames, so it lasts longer at 30 fps than at 144 fps (for example 12 frames is 0.4 s at 30 fps but about 0.083 s at 144 fps).

Gives a correct design: game code measures elapsed seconds since the hit (or stores the hit time), computes a progress value from 0 to 1, and sets a uniform that the shader uses to mix the tint, ending at exactly 0.
Addresses sharing: a uniform set on a material shared by several objects changes all of them, so a per-object copy of the material or a per-instance parameter is needed to pulse only the hit object.

questions.prompt: Trace one textured mesh through the rendering pipeline from the moment game code decides to draw it until a pixel changes colour on screen. Name the stages in order and say for each whether it runs on the CPU or GPU and whether developers program it or configure it. Explain where a fragment can still be rejected after the fragment shader has run, and what that means for performance.

rubric.text: The CPU side prepares the work: the game submits the mesh's vertex data, textures, uniform values and a draw command (draw call) to the GPU.
The vertex shader runs per vertex on the GPU, is programmable, and outputs a position (clip space) and values to pass on, such as UV.
Mapping to the screen and rasterization are fixed-function: they decide which pixel positions each triangle covers and produce a fragment for each, with interpolated values.
The fragment shader runs per fragment, is programmable, samples textures and outputs a colour and alpha, and may discard.

Depth and stencil tests and blending are configurable fixed-function steps that decide whether and how the output is written to the framebuffer, so a fragment can run the shader and still be rejected, which is wasted work (overdraw).

questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: "Make the character sprite look metallic and shiny." The game is 2D. Explain the difference between a 2D canvas shader and a 3D spatial shader in terms of what each one writes and who computes the final lighting, say what goes wrong with the instruction as worded, and rewrite it so the agent builds a convincing 2D result.

rubric.text: A 2D canvas shader works in 2D coordinates, and its fragment stage writes the final output colour of each pixel (typically starting from vertex colour times texture colour), as used for sprites, UI and tiles.

A 3D spatial shader works on meshes with 3D transforms, and its fragment stage sets material properties (albedo, roughness, metallic, emission, alpha) that the engine's lighting model turns into the final colour.

Explains the consequence: physically based terms such as roughness and metallic have no meaning in a 2D canvas shader, so "metallic" is ambiguous and an agent may try a 3D material on a sprite or invent parameters that do nothing.

Offers a feasible 2D approach, for example a moving highlight band computed from UV and time and masked by the sprite's alpha, a lit sprite using a normal map and 2D lights, or a colour ramp, and states that these fake the look.

Gives a rewritten instruction that names the shader kind and stage, the inputs (UV, time or a uniform), the mask (preserve alpha), and the intended look (for example a diagonal highlight sweeping every two seconds).

questions.prompt: A developer asks a coding agent for "flowing water" on a flat 2D tile that uses a 128 × 128 texture. Explain what UV coordinates are, what texture sampling does, and how a scrolling effect is made in a fragment shader. Specify the instruction you would give the agent so that it sets the sampler's repeat and filtering correctly, and describe two visible faults that appear if those settings are wrong.

rubric.text: Defines UV as 2D coordinates that map points on a surface to positions in a texture (normally 0 to 1), and texture sampling as reading the texture's colour at a UV, where one pixel of the texture is a texel.
Explains scrolling: add an offset proportional to time to the UV before sampling, with a speed in UV units per second (for example 0.25 per second repeats the pattern every 4 seconds).
Says the texture must be seamless and the wrap mode must be repeat, otherwise the offset UVs run past 0 to 1 and the edge texels are smeared (clamp) or a visible seam appears.
Chooses filtering deliberately: linear filtering for smooth water, nearest for crisp pixel art, and notes that sampling between texels with the wrong filter gives blur or shimmer.

Gives a precise instruction naming the stage (fragment), the clock (engine time is fine here because the flow is continuous), the speed uniform, the repeat and filter settings, and the seamless-texture requirement.

questions.prompt: In an interview you are asked: "What is albedo?" A developer then tells a coding agent: "Use this photo of a brick wall as the wall's colour texture." The photo was taken in strong afternoon sun and has a dark shadow across its left third. Define albedo precisely and say how it differs from the colour you see on screen. Explain what will look wrong in the game and why, and rewrite the instruction so that an agent and an artist would produce a correct result.

rubric.text: Defines albedo (base colour) as the colour a surface reflects diffusely, independent of the lighting, and says the colour on screen is albedo combined with lights, shadows, reflections and emission.
Explains that the photo contains baked lighting (a cast shadow and highlights) that is not part of the surface colour, so the engine's lighting stacks on top and the shading is applied twice.
Describes the visible symptoms: the shadow stays fixed on the wall when lights move or in a different lit room, and the wall looks dirty or unevenly lit in a way that cannot be controlled.
States the fix: remove the lighting from the image (delighting) or use an evenly lit or scanned albedo.
Gives a rewritten instruction that names the slot (albedo or base colour) and the requirement (no baked shadows or highlights in the image).

questions.source: Say it to the agent: shinier means roughness, metallic or specular
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: "Make the ship's hull look like polished steel and shinier." Explain roughness, metallic and specular and what each controls. Say which of them the agent should change, and which tempting changes (albedo, emission) would be wrong and why. Then rewrite the instruction with concrete parameter targets, and say what the scene needs in order for a smooth metal to look right.

rubric.text: Defines roughness (how blurred reflections are, 0 mirror-like and 1 fully blurred) and metallic (non-metal versus bare metal, where a metal's reflections take the base colour as their tint).

Defines specular (strength of reflection on non-metals) and states which controls the agent should change: "shinier" steel is done by lowering roughness and raising metallic toward 1, and specular is not the control for a metal.
Explains why the tempting changes are wrong: a lighter albedo makes the surface lighter, not glossier, and emission makes it glow rather than reflect.
Rewrites the instruction with concrete targets for the parameters (for example metallic near 1, roughness around 0.2 to 0.3, base colour a steel grey).
Says that a smooth metal needs an environment or reflection source in the scene to have anything to reflect.

questions.source: Normal map versus height or bump map
questions.prompt: An artist asks a coding agent to "add depth to the stone wall with a normal map", and also expects the stones to stick out of the wall's outline at an outside corner. Explain what a normal map is, how it differs from a height or bump map, and what a tangent-space normal map means. Say what a normal map can and cannot do for this wall, what the agent should do about the outline, and name two ways the normal map can be set up wrong and how each one looks.

rubric.text: Defines a normal map as an image storing a surface direction per texel (red, green, blue as x, y, z) that changes how light shades the surface without changing the geometry.
Contrasts it with a height or bump map, a greyscale elevation image from which slopes (or parallax or displacement) are derived, and notes only real displacement moves vertices.

Explains tangent space: directions are stored relative to the surface (x along U, y along V, z out of the surface), so the map works on any orientation, and a flat texel is the pale blue (128, 128, 255).
States that a normal map cannot change the silhouette, so stones sticking out at the corner need real geometry, tessellated displacement, or a parallax effect that only fakes depth.

Names two setup errors with their appearance, for example a flipped green channel (the engine expects the opposite Y convention) so bumps look like dents under light from above, or the map imported as sRGB colour so lighting is tilted and wrong.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between colour textures and data textures, and what sRGB and linear mean for them. Classify these five images: albedo, normal map, roughness, ambient occlusion, emission colour. For two of the wrong-flag mistakes, predict what the result looks like and give at least one number. Explain why this kind of mistake is hard to notice, and what the developer should say to a coding agent to prevent it.

rubric.text: Explains that colour images are stored in sRGB (steps spaced for human vision) and must be decoded to linear before lighting math, while data images store the numbers themselves and must be read as they are.
Classifies correctly: albedo and emission colour are colour (sRGB); normal map, roughness and ambient occlusion are data (linear).

Predicts the look of two wrong-flag mistakes and gives at least one number, for example a roughness value 0.50 decoded as sRGB becomes about 0.22 so the surface looks too glossy, a normal map decoded as sRGB tilts a flat surface by tens of degrees, or an albedo read as linear looks washed out and too bright.
Explains why the mistake is hard to notice: nothing fails or warns, the material still renders, and the result looks plausible but wrong in a way that depends on lighting.
Gives the instruction: say explicitly which maps are colour and which are data, ask the agent to set and report the colour-space import flag of each, and check the result under controlled lighting.

questions.prompt: A mobile 3D game has a long cobblestone road. Players see the road shimmer in the distance, and the game runs out of video memory on low-end phones. The scene uses 40 textures of 2048 × 2048 texels in RGBA8 (4 bytes per texel, 16 MiB each at the base level). Explain what mipmaps, texture filtering and texture compression are, and which of them address which problem. Calculate the memory before and after your proposed settings (a mip chain adds a third; assume a block-compressed format at 8 bits per texel), and state one cost of each choice.

rubric.text: Defines the three terms: mipmaps (a chain of pre-averaged half-size copies of a texture), texture filtering (how a value is computed between texels or over many texels: nearest, bilinear, trilinear, anisotropic) and block compression (a GPU format that stays compressed in video memory, unlike PNG or JPEG file size on disk).

Says which addresses which problem: the shimmer is minification aliasing (many texels per pixel in the distance), fixed by mipmaps with trilinear or anisotropic filtering, while the video-memory problem is addressed by compression, and mipmaps by themselves add memory.

Calculates the memory before: 40 × 16 MiB = 640 MiB at the base level (accepted as the starting figure, since a shimmering scene probably has no mipmaps yet), and about 853 MiB once full mip chains are added (one third more).
Calculates the memory after compression: 4 MiB per texture, 160 MiB for the 40 at the base level, about 213 MiB with mip chains.

States one cost per choice: mipmaps add about 33 percent memory, block compression is lossy (banding, artefacts, special handling for normal maps), and anisotropic filtering costs extra sampling time.

questions.prompt: A game has 40 enemies that share one mesh and one shader. The designer wants four colour variants, and a hit flash that affects only the enemy that was just hit. A coding agent was told: "Make a red version of the enemy material and flash the hit enemy." Define shader, material, texture and material instance. Design how the four variants and the single-enemy flash should be built, explain what happens if the agent edits the shared material, and map the idea to at least two engines.

rubric.text: Defines shader (the program), material (a shader plus parameter values and texture bindings assigned to a mesh), texture (image data a material reads) and material instance (a variant of a material that overrides parameters without a new shader program); the point is earned when at least three of the four definitions are correct.
Designs the variants as four materials or instances that share the one shader (and textures where possible), differing only in parameters such as tint.
Designs the hit flash as a per-object change: a per-object copy or dynamic instance, or a per-instance parameter, so only the hit enemy changes.
Explains the failure of the vague instruction: editing the shared material changes all 40 enemies at once because they all reference the same resource.

Maps the idea of a shared material versus a per-object copy, instance or parameter to at least two engines (for example Unity's shared versus per-renderer material, Unreal's constant versus dynamic material instances, Godot's duplicated material or per-instance shader uniform); exact API names are not required.

questions.prompt: A level has a 20 m × 20 m concrete floor and 30 small props (crates, barrels, signs), each with its own small texture. A developer tells a coding agent: "make the floor texture bigger and put all the prop textures together." Explain tiling, UV scale, texel density and seamless textures, and why "bigger" is ambiguous. Explain what a texture atlas is, what it gains, and two things that go wrong when textures are packed into one. Calculate the texel density for a 1024-texel texture stretched once across the floor and for the same texture repeated 10 times across it.

rubric.text: Explains tiling as repeating a seamless texture across a surface by scaling the UVs with a repeat wrap mode, and why a non-seamless texture shows joins.
Explains that "bigger" is ambiguous: bigger features (fewer repeats), a larger-resolution texture, or more repeats, each with a different effect on look and memory.

Calculates texel density correctly: 1024 texels over 20 m is about 51 texels per metre (blurry), and 10 repeats give 10,240 texels over 20 m, which is 512 per metre, at the cost of visible repetition.
Defines a texture atlas as many images packed into one texture with each mesh's UVs addressing its own region, so the props can share one material and reduce state changes and draw calls.

Names two problems of atlases: filtering and mipmaps bleed colour between neighbouring regions unless padded, and hardware repeat cannot tile a sub-region of an atlas; also acceptable are wasted space or the need to remap every prop's UVs.

questions.prompt: A developer reports to a coding agent: "The metal shield material is pure black, the crevice ambient occlusion has no effect, and the glowing crystal does not light the cave wall. The textures must be broken, so regenerate them." The scene has one directional light, no environment lighting or reflection source, and the ambient light is set to zero. Critique this diagnosis. Explain what each symptom really says about metal, ambient occlusion and emission, and describe the instruction and test you would give the agent instead.

rubric.text: Explains that a metal has no diffuse colour and shows only reflections, so with nothing to reflect (no environment or reflection probe) it looks black apart from the highlight of the light, which is a lighting problem and not a texture problem.

Explains that ambient occlusion by default affects only ambient light, so with ambient at zero and a strong direct light there is nothing for it to darken; it needs ambient or environment light, or a setting that lets it affect direct light, or a separate screen-space effect.
Explains that emission only makes the emissive surface itself glow, and that lighting the cave wall needs an actual light or a global-illumination technique that treats emissive surfaces as sources.
States the general principle that physically based materials are judged under stated lighting, so the same textures can look right or wrong depending on the scene.

Proposes a better instruction and test: place the material in a neutral lit environment (for example an environment map or reflection probe), compare it with the current scene, and regenerate textures only if they are still wrong.

questions.source: Evidence versus a claim of success
questions.prompt: A coding agent submits a change to a shader with the summary: "Compiles cleanly, all existing tests pass, verified." Explain the different kinds of evidence a reviewer can ask for, ordered from weakest to strongest, and say what each one can establish and what it cannot. Include at least one thing that only a person looking at a real screen, or a run on real graphics hardware, can establish. Also say how you would treat the word "verified" in the summary.

rubric.text: Identifies the compile or parse check as the weakest rung: it shows the source is valid (syntax and types) and says nothing about what the shader outputs.

Describes checks of the shader's contract and of the code that drives it (uniform names, types and defaults, and that game code sets the right values at the right moments), which can run without a display but still say nothing about pixels.

Describes a calculation of what the output should be for chosen inputs, worked out on the CPU from the specification, and notes it states the expected result, not what the GPU drew (this rung and the previous one may be given in either order).

Describes observation: rendering a fixed test scene, capturing it and comparing pixel values or a reference image, and says that only real hardware (or a person looking at a real screen) shows the driver, precision and timing behaviour of a real device (noting that a headless run with a dummy renderer gives no pixel evidence is welcome but not required).
Distinguishes a claim from evidence: asks which of the agent's statements were observed and which inferred, and treats "verified" with no named check or result as an unsupported claim.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: a precise shader specification
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction: "Add a damage flash to the player and make sure it works." Rewrite the instruction precisely, using the correct terms, so that the result can be checked. Then explain what the agent could build wrongly, or wrongly claim, if the original wording were used.

rubric.text: The rewrite names a shader parameter (a uniform) with a stated range and gives the output rule: at 0 the output equals the original colour exactly, at 1 it equals a named flash colour, in between a linear mix, with alpha unchanged (the point is earned when at least four of these five elements are present).
The rewrite states the timing in game time (seconds, from per-frame delta time) rather than in frames, gives a duration, and requires the same duration at different frame rates.
The rewrite states the trigger and the scope: the flash starts when the player is hit, applies to the player only, and returns to 0 when it ends.

The rewrite asks for specific evidence: a fixed test scene with known inputs, captured pixel values next to expected values, a check shown to fail on a known-bad version, and a report separating what was observed from what was assumed (the point is earned when at least three of these four elements are present).

Explains the consequences of the vague wording: the agent could count frames, mix against the wrong input, apply alpha twice, change a shared material so every sprite flashes, never reset the parameter, or report success from a clean compile alone.

questions.source: Specification oracle and testing the test
questions.prompt: An agent adds a test for a fade effect by recomputing the expected value with the same formula that appears in the shader. The test passes on a change that contains a real bug. Explain why it passes, what a better oracle would be, and how the developer can show that a new check can be trusted. Explain why a check run at a single setting, such as one frame rate, can mislead, and how to avoid that.

rubric.text: Defines a test oracle as what a test compares against, and explains why the test passes: an expected value copied from the shader's formula repeats the shader's mistake, so passing is circular.
Proposes an oracle written from the specification (endpoint values and the intended rule) and computed independently of the shader code.

Explains testing the test: run the check against a known-good and a known-bad version; it must pass the first and fail the second before its pass counts as evidence, and a failure on known-good code means the check itself may be wrong (for example a tolerance that is too tight).

Explains why a single setting can mislead: a correct and a wrong implementation can give the same result at that setting (for example a frame-counted fade and a time-based fade agree at exactly one frame rate).

Says the check should be run at several settings, chosen where right and wrong answers differ (for example 30, 60 and 144 frames per second); an illustrative worked example is welcome, such as a 33-frame counter lasting 0.55 s at 60 frames per second, 1.1 s at 30 and about 0.23 s at 144.

questions.source: Coordinate spaces and mixing them up
questions.prompt: Define local, world, view and screen space. Describe a bug caused by mixing two of them in a shader, the symptom a player or tester would see, a controlled test that would expose it, and what you would tell a coding agent to prevent it. (Any valid pair of spaces may be chosen.)

rubric.text: Defines all four spaces correctly: local relative to the object's origin, world shared by the scene, view relative to the camera, screen as the position on the display (usually pixels).

Gives a concrete mixed-space bug, such as comparing a local-space position with a world-space height, combining a local normal with a world-space light direction, or using a view-space position where a world-space one is meant.

Describes a symptom that matches the bug chosen: for a local-versus-world mix, the effect follows the object, rotates with it or depends on where the object was placed instead of staying fixed in the world; for a view-versus-world mix, it changes as the camera moves.

Describes a controlled test that varies what the chosen bug depends on (moving, rotating and scaling the object for a local-versus-world mix, moving the camera for a view-versus-world mix), because a trivial transform hides the bug; a student whose bug involves normals may cite the inverse transpose under non-uniform scale as the reason the test needs a non-uniform scale.

Says what to tell the agent: name the space of every input and output, require the conversion (for example "convert the position to world space with the model transform before comparing") and ask for a test at a non-trivial transform.

questions.source: Precision, branching and fragment cost on mobile
questions.prompt: A shader looks right and runs smoothly on the developer's desktop, but on a mid-range phone it shows stepping or flicker and the frame rate drops. Give four distinct possible causes involving precision, branching, fragment cost and platform differences, and explain how you would gather evidence for each rather than guessing, including on what hardware the measurements must be taken.

rubric.text: Precision: reduced (half) precision may really be used on the phone, so large values such as time or world position lose resolution; evidence comes from forcing full precision or testing at large values and comparing.
Branching: a condition that differs between neighbouring pixels makes the hardware run both sides; evidence comes from timing the shader with the branch removed or its condition made uniform.

Fragment cost: cost is pixels covered times layers times work per pixel; evidence comes from lowering the resolution and seeing whether frame time falls noticeably (close to proportionally if the shader is fragment-bound).
Measurements about the phone must come from the phone with a profiler, not from the desktop, a headless run or a software renderer.

Platform differences: the same shader can legitimately render differently across GPUs and drivers, so captures from the phone are compared with a reference for that platform within a stated tolerance.

questions.prompt: Design a golden-image (screenshot comparison) test process for a library of shaders. Cover what is rendered, how differences are judged, who approves a reference image, how different platforms are handled, and what a passing result does and does not prove.

rubric.text: Specifies a fixed test scene: fixed camera, resolution, inputs, pinned clock and no randomness, so any difference comes from the shader.
Requires a person to review and approve each reference image, and for any later update to be reviewed, because a reference captured from a buggy build bakes the bug in.

Sets a tolerance (per-channel difference and the share of pixels allowed to differ) and explains the trade-off: too tight gives false failures from driver differences, too loose hides small real defects.
Keeps separate references per platform, graphics API or colour space, because correct output can differ between them.

States the limits: a pass only means the output matches the baseline for what the scene exercises, not that it is right, and the process needs a renderer that actually draws pixels (not a dummy or headless driver), with real hardware needed to say anything about real devices.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: "an explosion" versus a precise burst
questions.prompt: In a 2D game, a developer tells a coding agent: "Add an explosion when the grenade hits." Rewrite this instruction precisely, using the correct particle-effect terms, and explain what the agent could build wrongly if it were given only the original wording.

rubric.text: Specifies a one-shot burst with a stated particle count born at one instant, rather than a looping emitter with a continuous rate.
Gives a lifetime in seconds and defines the motion: an initial speed range, a spread (range of launch directions) and gravity (or none).
Specifies the changes over lifetime, such as a scale curve to zero and a colour or alpha ramp that fades to transparent, read by normalised age.

Says where and when it plays, covering at least three of these four: at the grenade's position on the hit event; in world coordinates; as an object that is not hidden or destroyed with the grenade; with a size, texture or colour that makes each particle visible.
Names what the vague wording leaves open (looping forever, wrong position, particles too small or faint to see, no fade, never replaying on the next hit).

questions.prompt: A smoke effect must never have more than 240 particles alive at once. (a) Explain how emission rate, lifetime and the number of live particles are related. (b) With a lifetime of 3 seconds and continuous emission, what is the highest rate that stays within the limit? (c) A developer instead fires a burst of 100 particles every 0.5 seconds, each living 1.2 seconds. Work out the average and the peak number of live particles, and say whether the limit is met. (d) Describe two ways to fix the problem, and say what you would tell the coding agent.

rubric.text: States that the steady-state live count is emission rate times lifetime (births per second times seconds of life).
Computes the maximum continuous rate for a 3-second lifetime: 240 / 3 = 80 particles per second.
Computes the average for the burst case: (100 / 0.5) × 1.2 = 240 live particles.
Shows the peak is higher than the average: just after a burst three bursts overlap (ages 0, 0.5 and 1.0 seconds), giving 300 particles, so the limit is exceeded even though the average equals it.

Gives two fixes with their effect (for example a burst of 80, giving a peak of 240, or a lifetime of 0.9 seconds so at most two bursts overlap, giving 200) and tells the agent to treat the limit as a hard cap on peak live particles and to test the peak.

questions.prompt: A game has two effects. Effect 1 is ambient snowfall with 30,000 flakes that never affect gameplay. Effect 2 is 60 sparks from a collected coin, and each spark that touches the player adds to the score. Explain the difference between CPU particles and GPU particles, choose a kind for each effect, and defend each choice. Say what other factors you would check before settling the choice.

rubric.text: Defines the difference: CPU particles run the per-particle update on the CPU, GPU particles run it in shaders on the graphics card; both are drawn by the GPU.
Chooses GPU particles for the snow: the count is large, the effect is cosmetic, and no script needs per-particle state.

Handles the scoring sparks by keeping the gameplay out of the particle system (separate gameplay objects or checks do the touching and scoring, with particles used only for the look), because per-particle gameplay logic needs particle state that GPU particles do not give cheaply; CPU particles are also accepted where the student notes that this works only if the engine lets scripts read per-particle state.
Explains cost: CPU simulation cost grows roughly in proportion to particle count, while GPU simulation moves that cost to the graphics card; drawing cost (fill rate, overdraw) is paid in both.
Names checks before settling: target hardware support (CPU particles run on a wider range of devices), whether the engine offers a needed feature only on one kind, and measuring on the target device.

questions.prompt: Explain why a screen full of large, transparent smoke particles can be expensive even when there are only a few hundred of them. Define overdraw, give a numerical illustration of how the fragment count is found, and list four ways to reduce the cost. Say how you would confirm the cost on a phone.

rubric.text: Defines overdraw as the same screen pixel being shaded more than once by overlapping surfaces, and gives the fragment count as pixels covered per particle times the number of particles (for example 150 quads of 200 × 200 pixels give 6,000,000 fragment-shader runs).

Explains why transparency is costly: stacked transparent layers cannot be rejected early by the depth test, and each must be blended in turn onto the pixel, whereas hidden opaque surfaces can be skipped.
Notes that cost grows with the square of particle size (doubling width and height quadruples the fragments) and that transparent corners of a quad are still shaded.

Lists four levers, such as fewer particles, smaller particles, shorter lifetime (live count is rate times lifetime), a quad shape that hugs the visible puff, or lower-resolution rendering of the effect.
Says to confirm the cost by measuring on the target phone with a GPU profiler or an overdraw view rather than estimating.

questions.prompt: In a 2D game a rocket flies around the screen. A developer tells a coding agent: "Attach two particle effects to the rocket, an exhaust and a glowing aura." The exhaust should leave a trail behind the rocket; the aura should stay around it. Explain local versus world coordinates, say which one each effect needs, describe what would happen if they were swapped, and rewrite the instruction precisely.

rubric.text: Defines local coordinates (particle positions are relative to the emitter's transform, so they move and rotate with it) and world coordinates (a particle keeps its position in the scene once it is born).
Chooses world coordinates for the exhaust, because particles stay where they were born as the rocket moves, which forms the trail.
Chooses local coordinates for the aura, because its particles must move with the rocket.
Describes the swap: an exhaust in local coordinates is carried along as a rigid plume with no trail, and an aura in world coordinates is left behind and smears across the screen.
Rewrites the instruction so that each effect names its coordinate space (and ideally its rate, lifetime and parent), and explains that the vague wording leaves the space to the agent's default.

questions.prompt: A 3D game needs a campfire with flames and sparks, and a column of dark smoke above it. Explain additive blending and alpha blending, say which each effect should use, and justify the choices. Explain what billboarding is and why the particles here need it, and describe how you would state these choices to a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines alpha blending (result mixes particle and background by alpha, so drawing order matters) and additive blending (particle light is added to the background, so order does not matter).
Chooses additive blending for flames and sparks, because overlap brightens toward white and no sorting is needed; notes that colours are clamped, so many overlapping particles can burn out to white.
Chooses alpha blending for the dark smoke, because smoke must cover and darken what is behind it; adding a dark colour adds almost nothing, so additive smoke would be invisible.

Defines billboarding (flat quads turned each frame to face the camera) and explains why these particles need it: a flat flame or smoke quad would otherwise be seen edge-on as a thin line from some angles.
States the choices to the coding agent as explicit settings for each emitter (blend mode and billboarding, and for example rate, lifetime and colour ramp) rather than leaving them to defaults.

questions.source: Particle effects: evidence versus a claim of success
questions.prompt: A coding agent adds a death effect and reports: "Test passes: the burst is emitting after the hit." The test was run headless, with no window and no graphics card. Explain what that result does and does not establish. Separate visual intent, engine state and measured cost, say which of them the test can reach, and describe how you would verify the other parts, including how random numbers should be handled in the tests.

rubric.text: Separates three things: visual intent (what the effect should look like), state (what the engine reports, such as emitting, position and a finished signal) and cost (what the effect takes from the frame).
Says a headless test can reach state: whether the effect starts, where it is, whether it is visible in the tree, whether it ends and whether it plays again on a second hit.

Lists things "emitting" does not show, such as a hidden or destroyed parent, an off-screen position, zero alpha, the wrong layer, particles too small to see, or a burst that fires only once (any valid example counts).

Explains that headless runs measure CPU simulation at most; GPU simulation and drawing (fill rate, overdraw) need a real GPU on the target hardware with a profiler, and a person must look at the screen for the appearance.
Explains how random numbers are handled in the tests: fix the random seed and the time step so a burst repeats exactly and a failure can be reproduced.

questions.prompt: A studio must choose between sprite-sheet (frame-by-frame) animation and rig-based (skeletal) animation for two projects: a small pixel-art platformer with one hero, and a 3D action game with twelve characters that share a humanoid body. For each project, recommend a method and defend it. Your answer should explain what each method stores, what changes from one frame to the next, and how the two differ in memory and art cost, reuse, blending, scaling and look.

rubric.text: States what each method stores: a sprite sheet holds many drawn images (in a grid) plus data saying which to show and when, while a rig-based character holds a skeleton, art bound to it, and clips of bone transforms over time.
States what changes from frame to frame: the displayed image for a sprite sheet, versus the bone transforms (and therefore the pose of the attached mesh or parts) for a rig.

Compares memory and art cost: sprite-sheet cost grows with actions times directions times frames and each new character needs new drawings, while a rig costs more up front (model, skeleton, weights) but its clips are small and cheap to add.

Compares reuse, retargeting and blending: characters sharing a skeleton can share and blend clips, while drawn frames do not transfer between characters and cannot be blended into a true in-between pose.

Gives a defended recommendation for each project that also names the trade-offs of look and scaling (a fixed hand-drawn look and fixed pixel resolution for sprites, deformation and resolution-independent geometry for rigs).

questions.source: Say it to the agent: animate the walk
questions.prompt: A developer types this to a coding agent: 'animate the character walking'. The project contains a character, but the developer has not said whether the art is a sprite sheet or a rigged model. Explain what is wrong with the instruction. Then rewrite it twice, once for each kind of art, using the right terms, and explain what the agent could build wrongly if it guessed, and how you would check the result.

rubric.text: Identifies the core ambiguity: the instruction does not say whether the art is frame-by-frame images or a skeleton with bone transforms, so the agent must guess the whole method.
Gives a precise sprite-sheet version covering the grid (columns and rows or cell size), which cells make the walk and in what order, the frame rate, and whether it loops.
Gives a precise rig version covering the skeleton or model, the named walk clip, its loop mode, whether the motion is in place or uses root motion, and the playback speed or blend with other clips.
Describes plausible wrong builds from a wrong guess, such as slicing a sheet with the wrong grid, rotating bones that do not exist, moving the body twice, or playing the walk once instead of looping.
Says how the result should be checked, for example by stating the expected observable behaviour (frame order, loop length, speed) so the developer can verify it instead of trusting the agent.

questions.source: Keyframe, interpolation, easing, clip and tween
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a keyframe, interpolation and easing, using a door that rotates from 0 to 90 degrees over 1 second as your example. Then explain when a developer should use an authored animation clip and when a tween created in code, and give one example of each.

rubric.text: Defines a keyframe as an authored value at a chosen time (here 0 degrees at 0.0 s and 90 degrees at 1.0 s).
Defines interpolation as computing the in-between values from the keys, for example linearly reaching 45 degrees at 0.5 s.
Defines easing as shaping the speed profile of the interpolation (slow in, slow out, fast start) without changing the start value, the end value or the total duration.

Explains that an authored clip is made ahead of time, stored with the scene, and editable and scrubbable by a designer, while a tween is created in code to move a property from its current value to a target over a duration, which suits end values only known at runtime.
Gives a fitting example for each, such as a designed cutscene door or menu slide as a clip and a health bar easing to a new value or a camera zoom to a runtime target as a tween.

questions.source: Skeleton, rig, skinning and vertex weights
questions.prompt: Explain what a skeleton (armature), a rig, skinning and vertex weights are, and how they relate. A tester reports that when the character raises an arm, skin near the shoulder stretches in a long web toward the neck and the armpit collapses. Say which of these concepts is most likely involved, what probably went wrong, and how you would describe the problem to an artist or a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines a skeleton (armature) as a hierarchy of bones where moving a parent moves its children, and a rig as the whole posable setup, including the skeleton, the skin binding and controls or constraints.
Defines skinning as binding mesh vertices to bones, and vertex weights as per-vertex amounts of influence from each bone, normally summing to 1.
Diagnoses the problem as a weighting problem: vertices near the shoulder are influenced by the wrong bones or by too many bones, so they follow the neck or chest when the arm moves.

Proposes a fix such as repainting or limiting weights on those vertices and testing at extreme poses, noting that the symptom points first at the weights and that the animation clip's keys are unlikely to be the cause.
Describes the problem precisely, naming the bones involved, the vertices or vertex group affected, and the pose in which it appears.

questions.prompt: A character walks down uneven stairs, and its authored walk clip makes the feet hover above some steps and sink into others. Explain forward and inverse kinematics, why the clip alone fails here, and how you would fix it with IK. Then write the instruction you would give a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines forward kinematics as computing the end position (the foot) from joint rotations down a chain, and inverse kinematics as taking a target position for the end of the chain and solving for the joint rotations that reach it.
Explains the failure: the keyed rotations know nothing about the stair surface, so the foot goes where the keys put it.
Describes the fix: find the ground under each foot (for example with a ray or shape cast) and set the foot as an IK target for its leg chain.
Describes how the IK is applied: layered on top of the authored clip and not replacing it, with the hips height adjusted so that both feet can reach their targets.
Writes an instruction that names the leg chains (hip, knee, ankle), the knee direction (a pole or hint), the target source, when the IK applies, and how strongly it blends with the clip.

questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: 'make the character walk forward at 3 metres per second using the walk clip'. The walk clip was authored so that the root bone travels 1.2 metres forward in each 1.0 second loop. Explain root motion and in-place animation, say what could go wrong with this instruction, and rewrite it precisely.

rubric.text: Defines root motion as applying the root bone's movement in the clip to the character's position in the world, and in-place animation as a clip that poses the limbs without moving the character, leaving travel to code or physics.
Identifies the double-movement risk: if the code moves the body at 3 m/s and root motion is also applied, the character moves about 4.2 m/s.
Identifies the foot-sliding risk: if root motion is ignored and code moves at 3 m/s, the feet were planted for 1.2 m per loop, so they slide unless the playback speed or blend is changed.
Rewrites the instruction by choosing one authority, for example an in-place walk, code-set speed of 3 m/s, and playback speed scaled to match, or root motion as the authority with code reading it.
Gives the rewrite its numbers: the 3 m/s target, the clip's 1.2 m per 1.0 s loop, and the playback-speed factor of 3 / 1.2 = 2.5 that the agent should apply, so that nothing is left for it to guess.

questions.prompt: A script moves a platform by 2 units every time the engine draws a frame, and a tester finds that the platform is much faster on a 144 frames per second monitor than on a 60 frames per second one. Explain why, with numbers, how to fix it, and what frame-rate independence means for animation clips and for sprite-sheet frame rates. Write the instruction you would give a coding agent.

rubric.text: Explains that the movement is tied to the number of frames drawn, so the speed is 2 × 60 = 120 units per second at 60 frames per second and 2 × 144 = 288 units per second at 144.
Fixes it by defining the speed in units per second and multiplying by the time elapsed since the previous frame (delta time).
Defines frame-rate independence as results that depend on elapsed time and not on how many frames were drawn, which does not require locking the frame rate.

Explains that clips advance by time and have a playback speed scale, and that a sprite sheet's frame rate is the animation's own rate (for example 12 drawn frames per second shown across several rendered frames), separate from the rendering rate.
Writes an instruction that states the speed in units per second, requires scaling by delta time (or using the engine's fixed physics step), and forbids per-frame increments.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a sword swing's damage hitbox to be on only during the part of the swing where the blade is sweeping, and a whoosh sound to play at the start of that part. Explain what an animation event (a method track) is, why putting these on the clip is usually better than starting timers in code, and what can still go wrong. Write the instruction you would give a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines an animation event or method track as a function call keyed at a time on the clip's timeline, run when playback reaches that time.

Explains the benefit: the timing travels with the clip, so it stays aligned when the playback speed changes, the clip is retimed, or the clip is replaced, and a designer can move it without editing code.

Explains the weakness of code timers: they run on their own clock, independent of the clip's playback speed and of interruptions, so they drift from the visuals and duplicate timing knowledge in two places.

Names what can still go wrong, such as events firing on the update in which the playhead crosses the key (possibly a frame late), or never firing if the clip is cancelled early, so the hitbox must also be turned off when the state is exited or interrupted.
Writes an instruction that names the clip, the times or phases, the functions to call, and what must happen on cancel or interrupt.

questions.prompt: Playtesters say two things about a character: its run cycle 'hitches' once per loop, and switching from walk to run 'pops'. Explain the likely causes in each case and the fixes, for a sprite-sheet character and for a rig-based character. Then write the instruction you would give a coding agent to fix the loop.

rubric.text: Identifies the usual loop-seam cause: the last frame duplicates the first or does not lead naturally into it, so a pose repeats or jumps at the seam.
Gives fixes for the loop: drop the duplicated frame or adjust the end pose, and for a rig make the start and end values match with an appropriate loop mode.
Explains the pop on switching as an instant cut between two different poses.

Gives the fix for the pop: for a rig, cross-fade or blend the bone transforms over a short time or use a blend by speed, and for a sprite sheet, which cannot blend frames into a true in-between pose, switch at a matching point in the cycle or add transition frames.
Writes a precise instruction for the loop, such as the exact frames to play, the frame rate, and the loop mode, so the agent does not choose them.

questions.prompt: A teammate tracks a character's animation with four boolean flags (is_jumping, is_attacking, is_crouching, is_hurt) and a long chain of nested if statements. Explain what a state machine is (states, transitions and conditions) and why replacing the flags with one is useful. Cover how it changes reasoning, bugs and testing, using the four-flag example.

rubric.text: Defines a state machine as a set of named states with exactly one current state at a time, transitions that are the allowed routes between states, and conditions or parameters that decide when a transition fires.

Shows the flag problem with numbers: four independent booleans give 2^4 = 16 combinations, many of them meaningless (for example jumping, crouching and hurt together), whereas a state machine has only the states that were designed.
Explains that transitions are explicit, so what can follow what is written down and unlisted routes cannot happen, which is easier to reason about than a web of nested conditions.
Explains that bugs become visible: the current state is a single named value that can be logged or shown, so a stuck state or a wrong transition can be seen.
Explains testing: states and transitions can be enumerated, so each allowed transition (and the absence of forbidden ones) can be exercised, and a missing exit can be found by inspection.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: specifying a state machine
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: 'make the character animate when it moves'. The project has idle, walk, run and jump clips. Explain what the instruction leaves open and what the agent could get wrong. Then rewrite it as a precise specification of a state machine.
