rubric.text: Identifies open questions about the conditions: what counts as moving (a speed threshold), the speed at which walk becomes run, and whether airborne movement counts.
Identifies open questions about the structure: which states exist, which transitions exist between them, and what happens to states not mentioned (for example jump and fall).
Identifies open questions about presentation: cross-fade or cut, the length of the cross-fade, whether each clip loops or plays once, and interrupt behaviour.

Writes a precise specification in the form of rows, each giving from-state, to-state, condition (with numbers), cross-fade time and whether it may interrupt, and says that unlisted transitions must not exist.
Names plausible wrong builds from the vague version, such as flicker between walk and run around one speed, a landing that plays the idle pose in mid-air, or clips that never loop.

questions.source: Animation tree, state machine, blend tree and blend space
questions.prompt: A character needs these behaviours: it walks, jogs or sprints according to how far the stick is pushed; it jumps and falls; and it swings a sword that cannot be interrupted by movement. Explain how the words 'state machine', 'blend space', 'blend tree' and 'animation tree' relate, then design which behaviours should be states and which should be blends, and say how you would describe the design to a coding agent.

rubric.text: Defines a state machine as a graph in which one state is active at a time and transitions move between states, and a blend tree as a graph of nodes that mixes clips according to parameters.

Defines a blend space as mixing clips by a continuous position on one or two axes, and explains that an animation tree is the whole graph that plays clips through such nodes (called an Animator Controller in Unity or an Animation Blueprint in Unreal; any equivalent name is accepted), in which these parts can be nested (for example a state that holds a blend), so a state machine is one part of it and not a synonym for all of it.
Assigns walk, jog and sprint to a blend driven by a speed parameter, because speed varies continuously and the result should change smoothly.

Assigns jump, fall and the sword swing to states with defined transitions, because they are committed actions with their own entry, exit and interruption rules (the swing having no transition from movement input).

Describes the design to an agent precisely, naming the states, the parameter that drives the blend and its range, the transitions with conditions, and the nesting (for example a ground state containing the speed blend).

questions.prompt: A game runs physics at 120 ticks per second and updates its animation graph at 60 frames per second. With the jump key held, the character lands on one tick and jumps again on the next, and the animation graph stays in its 'fall' state while the character rises. Explain why this happens and why it happens only sometimes. Describe two fixes and a test that would catch it reliably.

rubric.text: Explains the sampling mismatch: 120 / 60 = 2 physics ticks per graph update, and the graph reads the floor condition only at its own update.
Explains that when the landing tick and the take-off tick fall inside one graph update, the graph never sees 'on floor', so it does not register the landing and stays in fall.
Explains why it is intermittent: it depends on which of the two ticks in a graph update the landing falls on, which depends on earlier timing.
Describes two fixes, such as a transition that reacts to rising while airborne, running the graph in the physics step, or pushing the state change from the movement code at the moment it happens.

Describes a test that drives real input (holding the jump key), checks the animation state against the physical state, and runs the sequence at both tick offsets so that the unlucky timing cannot be missed.

questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: 'when the player presses Space, switch to the jump state'. The character also has Hurt and Dead states. Explain what is wrong with driving the state from the key press, rewrite the instruction precisely, say what else could drive the jump state instead of the key press, and explain how interrupts and priority should be specified for hit reactions and death.

rubric.text: Explains that a press-only condition ignores whether the character can jump now, so jump may start while the character is stunned, airborne or dead.
Rewrites the transition with guards: Jump pressed, character on the floor and the current state allowing a jump.

Explains the alternative of driving animation from the physical state (leaving the floor with upward velocity) so that picture and movement agree even when the jump has another cause, such as a bounce pad.

Explains how to specify interrupts: Hurt can interrupt Attack by an explicit transition, Dead overrides every state (for example by a transition from any state or a rule evaluated first), and a missing transition forbids an interruption.
Explains that when several transitions are valid at the same moment the order or priority must be stated, since otherwise the engine or the agent chooses.

questions.source: Edge cases: stuck state, impossible transition, rapid input
questions.prompt: Describe three edge cases that commonly break a character's animation state machine: a stuck state, an impossible (missing) transition, and rapid input. For each, give the symptom a player sees, the likely cause, a fix, and a way to test for it.

rubric.text: Describes the stuck state: the symptom is a character frozen in a pose, and the cause is a state whose exit condition never becomes true (for example a flag nobody sets).

Describes the impossible transition: the symptom depends on the engine and call (the request is ignored, the state is forced directly, or the recorded state and the picture disagree), and the cause is a requested change that has no defined route.
Describes rapid input: the symptom is that repeated presses restart the action, stack up or are lost, and the cause is that no rule says what a press during the action should do.

Gives a fix for each case, stated precisely enough to instruct an agent: an exit tied to the clip end or to a condition the code really sets; a decision on whether the transition should exist, then adding or forbidding it explicitly; and a deliberately chosen policy for presses (ignore during the action, restart, or remember one press with a buffer).

Describes tests that use real input and check the state: log the current state over time, check that every state except a deliberate end state has an exit, and replay fast presses and check the result.

questions.source: Input buffering, cooldown and coyote time
questions.prompt: Define input buffering, cooldown and coyote time, and explain how each differs from the others. A game uses a 0.15 s input buffer, the next attack becomes available at t = 0.50 s, and the player presses Attack at t = 0.30 s, 0.40 s and 0.52 s. Treat each press separately, as if the other two had not happened, and say what happens at each press. Then explain the trade-off in choosing the buffer length.

rubric.text: Defines input buffering as remembering a press made slightly too early so it is used when the action becomes available, and cooldown as a minimum time between uses of an action.

Defines coyote time as a brief grace period after leaving the ground in which a jump is still accepted, and distinguishes it from buffering (forgiving late input versus early input) and from cooldown (restricting repeated use).
Works out the press at 0.30 s: it expires at 0.45 s, before 0.50 s, so it is lost.

Works out the presses at 0.40 s and 0.52 s, each taken on its own: 0.40 s is remembered until 0.55 s and starts the attack at 0.50 s, and 0.52 s starts an attack immediately because it is already available.

Explains the trade-off: too short a buffer drops presses and feels unresponsive, while too long a buffer queues unintended actions and feels sluggish or random, so the length is a design choice that should be stated in the instruction.

questions.source: Hitbox and hurtbox timing with animation events
questions.prompt: A melee attack clip has startup, active and recovery phases. Explain how animation events (or property tracks) should control the attacker's hitbox, and how the enemy's hurtbox fits in. Cover damaging an enemy only once per swing, what must happen if the attack is interrupted in the middle of its active phase, and what you would tell a coding agent to build.

rubric.text: Defines a hitbox as the attacker's damaging region and a hurtbox as the defender's vulnerable region, both normally detection shapes, with layers or masks keeping a character from hurting itself.
Explains that the hitbox is enabled only during the active phase, switched on and off by events or a property track in the clip, so its timing follows the animation and playback speed.
Explains that without a record of targets already hit, a hitbox that overlaps for several updates damages the same enemy repeatedly, so each swing keeps a list of enemies it has hit.
Explains that if the attack is interrupted before the 'off' event, the event never fires, so leaving or interrupting the state must also turn the hitbox off.
Writes an instruction naming the clip, the active window (frames or times), the hitbox and hurtbox roles and layers, the once-per-swing rule and the cleanup on interrupt.

questions.source: Single source of truth for character state
questions.prompt: A project already has a gameplay state machine in code. A coding agent is asked to 'add an animation state machine' and builds a second, separate machine that tracks its own states from the player's input. Explain what can go wrong, how you would instruct the agent instead, how you would test the result, and what that test cannot tell you.

rubric.text: Explains that two machines with their own rules and timing can disagree, so the picture shows one state while gameplay is in another.
Explains the single-source-of-truth design: gameplay state is the authority, and the animation machine reads it through parameters or events and does not decide gameplay outcomes such as damage.
Writes the instruction precisely, naming the existing states, the parameter or signal that carries each, which transitions the animation machine has, and a rule that it must not read raw input.
Describes a test that drives real input, compares the animation state with the gameplay state over time, and checks forbidden transitions.
Names what such a test does not establish, namely whether the motion looks and feels right, which still needs a person to play and judge.

questions.source: Wiring a game event to a sound
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction for a Godot game: "Add a click sound when the button is pressed." Rewrite it as a precise instruction using the correct audio terms, and explain what the agent could build wrongly or leave out because of the original wording. Your answer should say what must be true for the click to actually reach the mix, not only that it plays, and how you would check it, saying what automated checks can show and what only a listener can confirm.

rubric.text: Names the trigger precisely: the button's pressed signal is connected to a handler that calls play() on a stream player, so game logic, not the audio system, decides when the click starts.
Specifies the sound and its type: a short one-shot (non-looping) stream, played by a non-positional player because an interface sound has no place in the world.
Specifies the bus, such as an SFX bus that sends to Master, and notes that a muted or lowered bus along the route silences the click.
Specifies behavior the original leaves open: loudness in dB relative to the music, and what happens on rapid presses (restart the click or overlap, which is a polyphony choice).
Separates what automated checks can show (the handler fires, routing, level on the bus, muting) from what only a person with speakers can confirm (audible, balanced, not annoying).

questions.source: Trigger versus collider for events that start sounds
questions.prompt: A designer wants two things: (a) a coin that chimes and disappears when the player touches it, while the player passes straight through, and (b) a closed door that thuds when the player runs into it and stops the player. A developer asks a coding agent for "a collider that plays a sound" for both. Explain the difference between a trigger and a collider that matters here, say which object each of the two items needs, which event should start each sound, what receives that event, where the chime's player should live given that the coin disappears, and describe one way a continuously reported overlap can produce a bad sound.

rubric.text: States that a trigger detects overlap and reports an event without blocking movement, while a solid collider blocks and produces a collision response.
The coin is a trigger (an Area in Godot, a trigger collider in Unity, an overlap volume in Unreal), and the chime starts from its enter event.
The door is a solid collider, and the thud starts from a collision or contact event, optionally scaled by how hard the player hit it.

Notes that game logic (not the audio system) receives the event and calls the audio player, and that the chime's player must outlive the coin (not be its child), or removing the coin cuts the sound off.

Explains that a per-step overlap (stay) callback restarts the sound on every physics step while the player stands in the zone, producing a buzzing retrigger, and that starting on the enter event or guarding with a playing check avoids it.

questions.source: Audio bus, master bus, effects and ducking
questions.prompt: A game has music, sound effects and character voice, and a settings menu where the player can adjust each. Design the audio bus layout and explain it. Your answer should define a bus, the master bus and a bus effect, say how a menu slider should be turned into a level, and explain ducking and why putting everything on a single bus would be a poor design.

rubric.text: Defines a bus as a channel that sounds are routed to, with its own level, mute and effects, whose output is sent to a parent bus, and the master bus as the final bus that receives everything and ends the chain.
Proposes separate buses such as Music, SFX and Voice that each send to Master, so each can be balanced, muted and exposed to a slider independently.
Explains a bus effect, such as reverb or a low-pass filter, as processing applied to every sound routed through that bus, with an example of where it would be used.

Explains ducking as the automatic, temporary lowering of the music while voice plays, usually by a side-chain or mix rule, returning to normal afterwards, which is different from pausing or stopping the music.

Explains that decibels are logarithmic, so a linear slider value must be converted to dB (with the bottom of the slider mapping to a muted or very low level), and that with a single bus none of this independent control is possible.

questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: "Make the robot's footsteps 3D." Explain what positional (spatial) audio requires, using the terms listener, attenuation and audio stream player (the Godot node that plays sound; Unity's AudioSource and Unreal's audio component play the same role). Say what the agent could get wrong, and explain why the menu click and the background music should usually not be positional.

rubric.text: Explains that positional audio computes a sound's level and left-right placement from the position of the source relative to a listener.

Identifies the listener as the point that stands in for the player's ears, typically the active camera, and notes that one is active at a time per scene or viewport; an agent could leave it on the wrong object so everything is quiet or mis-panned.
Explains attenuation (falloff) as the loss of level with distance, optionally with a maximum distance beyond which the source is inaudible.
Says the sound source must be attached to the robot so it moves with it (a positional player that follows the node), and that the positional player type is chosen instead of the plain one.
Explains that interface sounds and music have no location in the world, so a positional player would make them quieter or panned depending on the camera; they use the non-positional player.

questions.prompt: Explain why a rhythm game should judge hits against the audio clock rather than accumulate frame time. Your answer should cover the audio mixing block, output latency and what happens when a hit sound is started, and then say what an automated test that runs with no sound device can and cannot establish about the game.

rubric.text: Explains that frame time varies with rendering load and runs on a different clock from the audio hardware, so time built from accumulated frame deltas drifts from the music being heard.
Explains that audio is mixed in blocks on its own clock, so the reported playback position advances in coarse steps and may be smoothed with another clock between updates.
Defines output latency as the delay between a sample being mixed and being heard, and says it should be compensated for or made adjustable, since the judgment should match what the player hears.
Says a sound begins at a mixing boundary, not at the instant play() is called, so a hit sound can be slightly late.

Says a test with no output device can check logic, routing, triggering and levels on a bus, but cannot prove the sound is audible, pleasant or lined up with the beat as heard, which needs a person with speakers or headphones.

questions.prompt: A developer's automated test for a hit sound asserts that the stream player's playing property is true right after the hit event and prints PASS. A reviewer says the test proves very little. Explain what the test does establish and what it does not, and list at least four additional checks, automated or by a person, that would make the evidence stronger.

rubric.text: States what the test shows: the hit event reached the handler and play() was called on that player at that moment, so the trigger path is wired.
States that it does not show which bus the sound went to or whether a muted or lowered bus swallows it.
States that the test is a single yes/no reading of the player's own flag, with no measurement of level or timing, so a true flag does not show that the sound ever reached the output.

Lists additional checks: a negative case (a miss stays silent), muting the bus removes the sound at Master, behavior on pause and on restart, and measuring the signal on the bus rather than reading a flag.
States that audibility, balance against the music and sync with the beat can only be judged by a person listening on real hardware.

questions.prompt: A shooter needs three sounds: a rapid gunshot (10 per second, each with an audible tail of 0.5 s), a rain ambience that plays for the whole level, and a car horn that honks while a key is held. For each, decide whether it should be a one-shot or a looping sound and what polyphony it needs. Explain polyphony, what a single-voice player does when triggered rapidly, what the developer should do when every voice is in use, and what the developer should watch for at a loop point.

rubric.text: Defines a one-shot as a sound that plays through once per trigger and stops, and a loop as a sound that repeats until stopped.

Defines polyphony as the number of voices (simultaneous instances) a player can sound at once, and explains that a single-voice player cuts off the oldest sound when triggered again, so rapid shots would chop each other's tails.
Computes or reasons that the gunshots need about 5 overlapping voices (10 shots per second multiplied by a 0.5 s tail) to let every tail finish, and treats the gunshot as a one-shot.

Treats the rain as a looping ambience whose loop points must be seamless (no click or audible gap at the seam), and gives a reasonable choice for the horn: a loop that starts on key down and stops on key up, or a one-shot per press, with the reason.
Notes that more voices cost mixing work, so a polyphony limit and a rule for which voice to drop (oldest or quietest) are a design decision.

questions.source: Profiling workflow and instructing an agent
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction: "Make the game faster." Rewrite it as a precise set of instructions using correct performance terms, and explain what the agent could do wrongly with the original wording.

rubric.text: Sets a measurable target on named hardware, such as a frame-time budget (16.7 ms at 60 Hz) on the target device, and asks for frame time in milliseconds rather than only FPS.
Requires profiling first to find the bottleneck (CPU-bound or GPU-bound, and which function or frame stage), before any code is changed.
Requires one change at a time, with the same scene and conditions measured before and after, using repeated runs, a warm-up period and a report of spread or percentiles rather than a single number.
Requires that behavior stays the same, checked by a test, and that readability and risk be weighed against the gain, stopping once the budget is met.

Explains the wrong outcomes the vague wording allows: optimizing something that is not the bottleneck, measuring in an editor or vsync-capped run, changing behavior, or adding complexity for no measured gain.

questions.prompt: A game runs at 25 ms per frame on a target device. Explain how you would find out whether the frame is CPU-bound or GPU-bound, using experiments and profiler readings, and give two kinds of fix for each case. Explain why a fix for one kind of bottleneck does nothing for the other, and what you do after applying a fix.

rubric.text: Defines CPU-bound (CPU-side work such as game logic, physics, culling and submitting draw calls sets the frame length) and GPU-bound (shading, fill rate and rendering work sets it), noting that in a pipeline the slower side sets frame time.

Describes a diagnostic experiment, such as lowering resolution (a faster frame suggests GPU pixel work, while an unchanged frame suggests the frame is not pixel-bound, which leaves the CPU or a vertex-bound GPU), or comparing CPU frame time to GPU time in a profiler to confirm.
Gives two CPU-side fixes such as fewer draw calls through batching or instancing, cheaper scripts or physics, updating less often, or object pooling.
Gives two GPU-side fixes such as reducing overdraw or fill rate, simpler shaders, lower resolution or texture compression.
Explains that speeding up the stage that is not the limit leaves frame time unchanged, and that after a fix the bottleneck may move, so the developer measures again.

questions.prompt: A scene draws 5,000 separate small objects, each with its own draw call, and is slow on the CPU even though the total triangle count is modest. Assume each draw call costs about 4 microseconds of CPU time. Explain what a draw call is, work out how much CPU time the calls consume per frame and compare it with a 60 Hz budget, and explain how batching and instancing reduce the cost and what each one requires.

rubric.text: Defines a draw call as a command from the CPU to the GPU to draw geometry with a given mesh, material and state.
Computes 5,000 x 4 microseconds = 20 ms per frame, which already exceeds the 16.7 ms budget at 60 Hz, regardless of triangle count.
Explains batching as combining geometry that shares a material (and a texture atlas) into fewer draw calls, and states that it requires the combined objects to share that material.
Explains instancing as drawing many copies of one mesh with one material in a single call with per-instance data such as transforms, and states that it needs identical mesh and material.

States the effect on the cost: the saving comes from submitting far fewer calls, not from drawing fewer triangles, so if the 5,000 objects became 10 draw calls the call overhead would fall from 20 ms to 10 x 4 microseconds = 40 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A shooter creates a new bullet object for every shot and destroys it on impact, and the game stutters. A developer asks a coding agent to "pool the bullets". Explain object pooling and why it can help, describe the operations a pool needs and the per-object state that must be handled on reuse, and explain how to choose the pool size and handle a pool that runs out. Also state when pooling would not be worth it. Use 20 shots per second and a bullet lifetime of at most 3 seconds as your numbers.

rubric.text: Defines pooling as creating objects in advance and reusing them instead of creating and destroying them, and explains the benefit: less allocation cost and, where a garbage collector is used, less garbage and fewer collection hitches.
Describes acquire and release operations, and that an inactive pooled object is hidden and has processing and collision disabled.
Requires a full reset of reused objects (position, velocity, timers, ownership, hit flags) so stale state does not leak into the next use.
Sizes the pool from peak demand, about 20 x 3 = 60 bullets alive at once, plus margin, and gives a policy for exhaustion such as growing the pool, skipping the shot or recycling the oldest bullet.

States when pooling would not be worth it: when a profile shows no spawn, destroy or collection cost, or when the objects are few or long-lived; naming costs such as idle memory, extra complexity or releasing an object twice is welcome but not required.

questions.prompt: A developer says: "I ran it once and version B was 20 percent faster than version A, so we are switching." Critique this claim, then describe a sound way to benchmark the two versions and say what you would be entitled to claim afterward.

rubric.text: Explains that a single run cannot separate a real effect from run-to-run noise (other processes, thermal effects, scheduling), so the benchmark should be repeated and the spread reported.
Requires a warm-up period to be discarded, since start-up work such as shader compilation, caching and loading is not steady-state cost.

Requires identical conditions: same build type (release, not an editor or debug build), same hardware, same scene and inputs, vertical sync off or frame work measured directly, and only one variable changed.
Says to measure frame time in milliseconds and report mean or median plus a percentile or worst frame, not FPS alone, because averages hide hitches.
Limits the claim to what was measured: the hardware and workload tested, with a check that behavior is identical, and a judgment of whether the gain matters against the frame budget.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to rewrite a gameplay system into a more complex data layout to save an estimated 0.2 ms per frame. The game targets 60 Hz and currently takes 12 ms per frame on the target device. Decide whether to approve the rewrite, using the idea of premature optimization and the frame budget, and say under what conditions you would change your answer.

rubric.text: Defines premature optimization as optimizing before measurement shows a need, so the effort may not target a real bottleneck.

Uses the arithmetic: the 60 Hz budget is 16.7 ms and the game uses 12 ms, leaving about 4.7 ms of headroom, so 0.2 ms is about 1 percent of the budget and does not change whether the game meets its target.
Names the costs of the rewrite: complexity, readability, bug risk and maintenance burden.

Gives conditions that would justify it: a profile on the target hardware showing it is a hotspot, a projected increase in load (more entities), a weaker target device, or a frame budget that is currently exceeded.
Gives a clear decision (do not approve the rewrite now) and notes that the 0.2 ms saving is only an estimate that would have to be measured before it counts.

questions.prompt: A mobile game uses 40 textures of 2048 x 2048 pixels, each RGBA with 4 bytes per pixel and a full mipmap chain (which adds a third on top of the base level), stored uncompressed on the GPU. The game runs out of memory on the target phone. Calculate the texture memory, explain why the size of the image files on disk is not the number that matters, and propose and compare ways to reduce it. Take 1 MiB as 1,048,576 bytes.

rubric.text: Computes one texture as 2048 x 2048 x 4 = 16 MiB, about 21.3 MiB with the mipmap chain, and the 40 textures as about 853 MiB.
Explains that a PNG or JPEG on disk is compressed for storage, while the GPU needs pixels in a samplable format, so memory depends on resolution, bytes per pixel and format rather than the file size.
Proposes GPU texture compression, noting that a format at 1 byte per pixel cuts each texture to about 5.3 MiB (about 213 MiB in total).

Proposes reducing resolution where detail is not visible, since halving each dimension leaves a quarter of the memory (1024 x 1024 compressed is about 1.33 MiB each, about 53 MiB in total), and other options such as packing textures into atlases, sharing textures, or streaming.
Compares the options by their quality cost: compression can introduce visible artifacts, and lower resolution loses detail wherever it is seen.

questions.source: Saying it to the agent: NPC behavior
questions.prompt: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction: "Add enemy AI to the game." Rewrite it as a precise instruction for a guard that patrols, notices the player and chases, using the correct AI terms (including how the guard moves around walls and how it avoids switching rapidly between states), and explain what the agent could build wrongly from the original wording and how you would test the result.

rubric.text: Names the decision structure, such as a finite state machine (or behavior tree) with named states such as Patrol and Chase (a Search state is optional), and gives an explicit table of transitions with their conditions.

Defines perception precisely: a sight range and a line-of-sight check that walls can block (a field-of-view cone, hearing, and a remembered last known position kept in a blackboard or similar memory, are optional extras).
Specifies movement through pathfinding on a grid or navigation mesh with steering and obstacle avoidance, rather than moving in a straight line toward the player.
Prevents flicker at state boundaries, for example by using a larger radius to leave Chase than to enter it (hysteresis) or by using timers.

Gives a testable contract, such as exposing the current state name so a test can read it, and explains the wrong results the vague wording allows, such as an omniscient straight-line chaser that ignores walls.

questions.source: FSM, behavior tree, utility AI and GOAP
questions.prompt: A game has three NPCs: (a) a door guard that patrols, chases and searches, (b) a boss with several phases and many attacks that can interrupt one another, and (c) a villager who balances hunger, tiredness and work through the day. For each, choose among a finite state machine, a behavior tree, utility AI and goal-oriented action planning (GOAP), and defend your choices. Explain how each of the four architectures makes decisions and what it costs.

rubric.text: Explains a finite state machine (one current state, transitions on edges between states), its strength with a few distinct modes, and its cost: transitions multiply as states are added.

Explains a behavior tree (ticked from the root, nodes return success, failure or running, selectors and sequences, priority by order), its strength in reactive, composable branches, and a cost such as the priority ordering that must be authored and maintained.

Explains utility AI (scoring candidate actions from numeric considerations and picking the highest), its strength with continuous competing needs, and a cost such as scores that must be tuned and are hard to predict.

Explains GOAP (actions with preconditions and effects, and a planner that searches for a sequence reaching a goal) and gives its trade-off: flexible and emergent sequences, but harder to debug and more costly to run.

Assigns an architecture to each of the three NPCs and defends each choice consistently with the architectures as explained, using trade-offs such as designer control, debuggability, authoring effort and run-time cost, rather than naming a single best architecture; any assignment defended this way earns the point (for example a finite state machine or behavior tree for the guard, a behavior tree for the boss, utility AI or GOAP for the villager).

questions.source: Pathfinding: grid, A*, navmesh and steering
questions.prompt: A developer tells a coding agent: "Each frame, move the enemy toward the player." In a level with walls the enemy gets stuck against the first wall. Explain why, and describe how pathfinding fixes it. Your answer should cover the difference between a grid and a navigation mesh, how A* chooses its path and what an admissible heuristic does, how steering relates to the path, and one case where pathfinding can fail.

rubric.text: Explains that moving straight toward the target ignores obstacles, so the enemy pushes into a wall; reaching a target around walls needs a path computed over a representation of walkable space.
Contrasts a grid (cells marked free or blocked, simple, many nodes) with a navigation mesh (polygons covering walkable surface, fewer nodes in open areas, baked from geometry and agent size).
Explains A* as a search that expands nodes by f = g + h (cost so far plus estimated remaining cost), and that an admissible heuristic, one that never overestimates, lets it return a shortest path.
Explains that the path is a list of waypoints, that steering follows it and handles local avoidance each frame.

Names a failure case to handle, such as an unreachable target, a map that has not finished building, a stale navigation mesh after geometry changes, or an agent radius that is too large for a passage.

questions.source: Perception: sight, hearing and the blackboard
questions.prompt: Design how a guard NPC should see and hear the player. Explain the checks involved in sight, how hearing differs, what the guard should remember, and why an NPC that simply reads the player's position every frame is a poor design. Include one pitfall and how to avoid it.

rubric.text: Describes sight as three checks: distance within range, direction inside a field-of-view cone (the dot product of facing and direction to target compared with the cosine of the half-angle), and a line-of-sight test such as a raycast that walls can block.
Describes hearing as an event with a position and loudness that NPCs within hearing range react to, often reduced by distance or obstacles, rather than a continuous scan.
Describes memory: the last known position or sound location is stored (for example in a blackboard), drives a Search behavior, and expires after a time.
Explains that reading the player's position directly makes the NPC omniscient and unfair, breaks stealth gameplay, and removes the point of perception, which exists to limit what the NPC knows.

Names a pitfall with a remedy: flicker at the edge of the sight range (fixed with hysteresis), the cost of casting rays every frame (reduce or stagger the checks), or tuning for fairness through playtesting.

questions.source: Procedural generation: seed, noise, determinism and constraints
questions.prompt: A developer says: "Our level generator is random, so we cannot test it." Critique this claim. Explain how a seed, determinism and noise work in procedural generation, how constraints and a validator make generated content playable, and what such a validator can and cannot establish.

rubric.text: Explains that a pseudo-random generator is deterministic given its seed, so the same seed with the same algorithm produces the same output, and tests can fix seeds and compare results.

States what reproducibility requires: all randomness drawn from one seeded generator in a stable order, no clock-based seeds, and awareness that a change in the engine's generator can change results across versions, so data that must persist should be stored.
Explains coherent noise (Perlin, simplex or value noise, optionally with several octaves) as smooth variation that suits terrain, in contrast to white noise, which looks like static.

Explains constraints and validation: playability rules such as reachability from the player's real jump limits, generate-and-test (reject and re-roll) versus constructive generation, testing many seeds and hand-built bad cases, and keeping a safety margin.
Limits what the validator proves: it is a model of the game's rules, so it cannot show that a level is fun or that its model matches the real physics, and human playtests remain necessary.

questions.prompt: Explain reinforcement learning at an overview level using an NPC example, defining agent, environment, reward and policy. Describe how reward design can go wrong, how training differs from using the trained NPC in a game, and when a designer would choose reinforcement learning over a scripted state machine or behavior tree.

rubric.text: Defines agent (the NPC that acts), environment (the world and its rules that respond to actions), reward (a numeric feedback signal) and policy (the rule mapping observations to actions) with a concrete example.
Explains that the agent learns by trial and error from reward rather than from labeled correct answers.

Explains that reward design is hard: a reward can be too sparse to learn from, and an agent can exploit a loophole that scores well without doing what the designer meant (reward hacking), so shaping needs care and the result must be inspected.

Distinguishes training (many simulated episodes, costly, needs a fast simulator) from deployment (the trained policy typically runs as a fixed decision function in the game, with no learning during play).

Compares with scripted AI: RL suits behavior that is hard to hand-script, but designers cannot directly author or easily debug it or guarantee its behavior, so a state machine or behavior tree is the better choice when control and predictability matter.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a crowd of 100 pedestrians that walk to destinations and avoid bumping into each other. Explain how steering behaviors (such as seek, arrive, separation and obstacle avoidance) and pathfinding divide the work, how the behaviors are combined, what emergent behavior is, and why emergent results are hard to guarantee.

rubric.text: Defines steering behaviors as per-frame adjustments to an agent's velocity or force toward a goal or away from hazards, naming examples such as seek, arrive (slow down near the target), separation and obstacle avoidance.
Explains the division of labor: pathfinding provides the global route around static obstacles, while steering follows the route and reacts locally to moving things such as other pedestrians.
Explains that several steering outputs are combined, for example by a weighted sum, and that the weights are tuned to give the desired balance.
Defines emergent behavior as global patterns, such as lanes forming in a crowd, that arise from local rules and interactions without being coded directly.

Explains why it is hard to guarantee: outcomes are sensitive to parameters and conditions and cannot be predicted without simulation, so they need testing, measurement and playtesting, and can include unwanted cases such as jams or deadlocks.
